UNIT.subject: Essential Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Similarity between objects — identifying and sorting similar figures from the environment
• Properties of similar figures — corresponding angles and proportional sides
• Centre of enlargement — locating and tracing the centre on plain paper
• Linear scale factor — measuring corresponding sides and computing the ratio
• Drawing the image of an object given the centre of enlargement and linear scale factor
• Area scale factor — relating the ratio of image area to object area
• Volume scale factor — relating the ratio of volumes of similar solids
• Relationship between linear scale factor, area scale factor and volume scale factor
• Application of similarity and enlargement in real-life situations
• Project: making similar containers (cubes, cuboids, cylinders) of different sizes using locally available materials
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify properties of similar figures,
b) determine the centre of enlargement and the linear scale factor of similar figures,
c) draw the image of an object given the centre of enlargement and the linear scale factor,
d) determine the area scale factor of similar figures,
e) determine the volume scale factor of similar objects,
f) relate linear scale factor to area and volume scale factor of similar objects,
g) apply similarity and enlargement to real-life situations,
h) appreciate the use of similarity and enlargement in real-life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Digital Literacy: The learner develops the skills of connecting and interacting with digital technology when using digital resources (e.g., the Kenya Education Cloud or learner digital devices) to manipulate objects or figures — zooming or shrinking sizes — and to learn more on the application of similarity and enlargement in real life.
• Creativity and Imagination: The learner acquires networking and connection skills when drawing images of given objects under a particular enlargement scale factor and when designing and constructing similar containers of different sizes during the project.
UNIT.values: • Responsibility: The learner takes care of objects and containers collected from the immediate environment (e.g., packaging tins, juice cartons, sufuria lids) and of instruments used during construction and measurement tasks.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: Learners observe similar objects from the Kenyan environment (e.g., different-sized Kimbo tins, uji cups, water jerricans) and pose questions about what makes two objects truly similar and how one can be obtained from the other.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: Learners systematically measure corresponding sides of similar figures, record data in tables, and compute linear, area, and volume scale factors to test their predictions.
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: Learners apply ratios, proportions, and algebraic relationships to determine scale factors and to verify the relationship k² (area) and k³ (volume) from the linear scale factor k.
• Constructing Explanations: Learners use measurements and computed scale factors to explain why two containers hold volumes in the ratio k³ and to justify their model-building decisions during the project.
• Obtaining, Evaluating, and Communicating Information: Learners use digital devices and print resources to research real-life applications of similarity and enlargement (e.g., architectural scale drawings, mapmaking, photography) and present findings to peers.
UNIT.pcis: • Environment and Technology: The learner acquires the skill of sorting and responsibly managing the environment after collecting and sorting objects and containers from the immediate surroundings, and uses digital devices appropriately to explore enlargement.
UNIT.careers:
• Architecture and Building Construction: Scale drawings of buildings, rooms, and urban plans in Nairobi or Mombasa rely directly on similarity and linear scale factors.
• Cartography and Geography: Map-making for Kenya's counties and national parks uses enlargement and scale factors to represent large real-world distances on paper.
• Photography and Media Technology: Zooming in or out on images and resizing photographs for print or digital media applies area scale factor relationships.
• Fashion and Textile Design: Pattern grading — scaling clothing patterns up or down for different body sizes — uses the principles of similarity.
• Sports Management and Coaching: Designing scaled models of pitches, courts, and arenas (e.g., Kasarani Stadium layouts) involves enlargement and similarity.
• Hospitality Industry: Scaling recipes (e.g., ugali, mandazi, pilau) for different numbers of guests and resizing baking tins relies on volume scale factor reasoning.
• Engineering and Manufacturing: Producing components in different sizes (e.g., machine parts, water tanks, grain silos in the Rift Valley) requires precise application of linear, area, and volume scale factors.
UNIT.focus: This unit develops learners' understanding of geometric similarity and enlargement by anchoring instruction in tangible, Kenya-relevant objects — from differently-sized cooking pots and juice containers to architectural scale drawings. Learners move progressively from identifying properties of similar figures, through computing linear, area, and volume scale factors, to constructing their own similar containers as a project. Throughout, digital tools and hands-on measurement tasks are used to build both conceptual understanding and practical competence in applying similarity and enlargement to real-life situations.
UNIT.phenomenon:
ANCHORING PHENOMENON — "The Shrinking Uji Cup":
A teacher brings to class three different-sized cylindrical uji (porridge) cups — a small cup used by a toddler, a standard adult mug, and a large catering flask — all made by the same manufacturer and clearly sharing the same shape. When learners measure the height and diameter of each cup they discover that every dimension of the larger cup is exactly twice (or three times) the corresponding dimension of the smaller cup. Yet when they fill the small cup with water and try to fill the medium cup, they need FOUR small cups of water — not two. And to fill the large cup they need NINE small cups — not three. The numbers are puzzling: if the cup is "twice as big," why does it hold four times as much water in cross-section and apparently more in volume? Students are also surprised to find that the label (surface area) of the large cup requires NINE times as much paper as the small cup, not three times. This observable, countable mystery — that scaling lengths by k scales areas by k² and volumes by k³ — anchors the entire unit and drives learners to build a mathematical model that explains and predicts these relationships for any similar figures or solids.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• Differently-sized sufuria (cooking pots) used in a Kenyan kitchen: learners observe that a sufuria with double the diameter holds roughly eight times as much ugali, prompting the need to relate linear scale factor to volume scale factor.
• Aerial vs. ground-level photographs of Uhuru Park, Nairobi: a photograph taken from a drone at twice the altitude produces an image in which the park appears one-quarter the size — illustrating the area scale factor k² in a real mapping context.
• Architectural scale drawings of a school classroom: a builder's blueprint drawn at a scale of 1:50 shows how every length on paper relates to the real dimension, and learners calculate actual room areas and volumes from the drawing, reinforcing all three scale factors.
• Packaging of Cowboy or Kasuku cooking fat: the small, medium, and large tins are geometrically similar; learners compare their masses (proportional to volume) and label areas to verify k², k³ relationships using real consumer products found in Kenyan shops.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much — and how can we use this mathematical pattern to design, build, and predict the properties of any similar shape or object?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTION:
1. How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — Noticing Similarity (Predict & Observe): Learners collect objects and containers from their immediate environment (tins, cups, boxes). Working in groups, they sort objects they believe are "similar" and record their sorting rules. The teacher introduces the anchoring phenomenon (the three uji cups) and learners predict: if one cup is twice as tall as another, how many small cups of water will fill the big one? Predictions are recorded on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Learners then measure corresponding sides of sorted similar objects, observe that angles are equal and side ratios are constant, and formalise the properties of similar figures.

Lesson 2 — Centre of Enlargement and Linear Scale Factor (Observe & Explain): Learners trace an object and its image on plain paper and physically locate the centre of enlargement by drawing lines through corresponding vertices. They measure corresponding sides and compute the linear scale factor k. Multiple examples (different objects, different positions of the centre) consolidate understanding. Learners update the DQB with what they now know about how enlargement works.

Lesson 3 — Drawing Enlargements (Explain & Apply): Given a centre of enlargement and a linear scale factor (k = 2, 3, ½), learners construct the image of a given figure step by step. They verify their constructions by measuring. The teacher connects this to real-life contexts: a photographer in Mombasa enlarging a portrait, or a cartographer scaling a map of Kisumu. Learners discuss: does the shape change? Does the angle change? Does size change? They refine their DQB entries.

Lesson 4 — Area Scale Factor (Observe & Explain): Learners use cut-out squares and rectangles (similar figures of known dimensions) to compute the area of an object and its image. They tabulate ratios of areas for k = 2, 3, 4 and discover the pattern: area scale factor = k². The teacher returns to the anchoring phenomenon — the uji cups — and learners explain why four small cups of water fill the cross-section of the medium cup. Model revision: learners add the k² relationship to their cumulative class diagram on the DQB.

Lesson 5 — Volume Scale Factor (Observe & Explain): Learners use model cubes and cuboids of different sizes (or containers such as small and large Kasuku tins) to measure dimensions, compute volumes, and tabulate the ratio of volumes for k = 2, 3. They discover the pattern: volume scale factor = k³. They explain the anchoring phenomenon fully — why the large uji cup needs nine small cups of water. Learners also connect to the sufuria supporting phenomenon. DQB is updated with k³.

Lesson 6 — Relating Linear, Area and Volume Scale Factors (Explain & Model Building): Learners consolidate all three relationships (k, k², k³) using a unified table. They solve mixed problems: given that two similar water tanks in the Rift Valley have a linear scale factor of 3, find how many times more paint is needed for the larger tank (k² = 9) and how many times more water it holds (k³ = 27). Digital devices are used to explore and verify. Learners build a complete annotated model (diagram + formula summary) in their notebooks and on the class DQB.

Lesson 7 — Real-Life Applications and Problem Solving (Apply & Communicate): Learners apply similarity and enlargement to multi-step real-life problems: scale drawings of school buildings, resizing recipes (e.g., scaling a mandazi recipe for a school party — doubling the tin size means eight times the dough), and map reading. Learners use digital or print resources to find additional examples and present one finding to the class. The driving question is revisited and learners articulate a full answer supported by evidence.

Lesson 8 — Project Presentations and Assessment (Model Building & Evaluation): Learners present their project: similar containers (cubes, cuboids, cylinders) constructed from locally available materials in at least two different sizes. They demonstrate measurement of dimensions, calculation of linear, area, and volume scale factors, and document challenges. Peers and the teacher use a rating scale for assessment. The class DQB is reviewed and completed — all sub-questions raised in Lesson 1 are answered. A written class activity consolidates individual assessment of all learning outcomes.

slo.purpose: Learners encounter the anchoring phenomenon — the three differently-sized uji cups — make and record predictions about how much water each holds, then sort and measure everyday objects to formalise the two defining properties of similar figures: equal corresponding angles and constant ratios of corresponding sides.
slo.knowledge:
• Define similar figures as shapes that have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides.
• State that the constant ratio of corresponding sides is called the linear scale factor (k).
• Identify pairs of similar figures from a collection of everyday objects and containers.
slo.skills:
• Measure corresponding lengths of objects using a ruler and record data in a table.
• Calculate the ratio of corresponding sides to determine whether two figures are similar.
• Sort a collection of objects into 'similar' and 'not similar' groups and justify the sorting rule.
slo.attitudes:
• Show curiosity and open-mindedness when predictions about water volume do not match observations.
• Appreciate that mathematical patterns — such as similarity — are embedded in everyday Kenyan objects and manufactured goods.
slo.keyInquiry: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This opening lesson launches the unit storyline by placing the anchoring phenomenon — three same-shape uji cups of different sizes — in front of learners. It surfaces prior knowledge through prediction, establishes the two formal properties of similar figures through hands-on measurement of familiar objects, and opens the Driving Question Board with the central mystery: if a cup is twice as tall, why does it hold four times as much water?
slo.safetyNotes: Handle glass or ceramic cups carefully to avoid breakage. If plastic cups are used, ensure they are clean. Water used for the volume demonstration should be disposed of in the sink or outside — not left as a slip hazard on the floor.

LESSONS.overview:
This is the first lesson of the Similarity and Enlargement unit and its primary purpose is to launch the anchoring phenomenon and open the mathematical inquiry that will run through all subsequent lessons. The teacher introduces three cylindrical uji (porridge) cups — a small toddler cup, a standard adult mug, and a large catering flask — all clearly manufactured to the same shape by the same maker, so that every dimension of the medium cup is exactly twice that of the small cup and every dimension of the large cup is exactly three times that of the small cup. Before any measurements are taken, learners predict in writing how many small cups of water will be needed to fill the medium and large cups. Most learners predict two and three respectively, mirroring the linear scale. The dramatic moment comes when the teacher actually fills the cups with water and learners count four small cups to fill the medium and nine to fill the large — numbers that contradict every intuitive prediction and immediately generate genuine mathematical puzzlement.

The lesson then grounds this puzzlement in the formal language of similarity. Working in groups of four, learners collect everyday objects from around the classroom and their bags — exercise book covers, tins of Kimbo or Blue Band, matchboxes, mobile phone boxes — and sort them into groups they believe are "similar." Each group records the rule they used to decide similarity. The teacher guides groups to test their rules by measuring corresponding sides with a ruler and comparing corresponding angles with a protractor or the corner of a sheet of paper. Through this structured measurement activity learners discover for themselves that similar figures share two measurable properties: corresponding angles are equal and the ratios of corresponding sides are constant. These two properties become the formal definition that the class agrees on and records.

By the end of the lesson learners have encountered the phenomenon, articulated an initial (and incorrect) prediction, begun to see why the prediction fails, and established the foundational vocabulary — similar figures, corresponding sides, corresponding angles, linear scale factor — that every later lesson will build upon. The Driving Question Board is opened with learner-generated questions, and learners produce their first annotated sketch model showing two similar rectangles with labelled corresponding sides and the ratio calculation. This model will be revised in every subsequent lesson as understanding deepens.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a sticky note. The teacher displays the three uji cups at the front of the room and asks learners to study them silently for 30 seconds, then write TWO predictions: (1) How many small cups of water will fill the medium cup? (2) How many small cups of water will fill the large cup? Learners write their predictions individually, fold the sticky note, and hold it until instructed to share. They then share predictions with a shoulder partner before the teacher collects a class sample by cold-calling.
framework.teacherMoves: Place the three cups on a tray at the front where every learner can see them clearly. Say: 'Look carefully at these three uji cups. They were made by the same factory — same shape, just different sizes. The medium cup is exactly twice as tall and twice as wide as the small cup. The large cup is exactly three times as tall and three times as wide.' Pause 10 seconds. Then say: 'On your sticky note, write your name and answer these two questions: One — how many small cups of water will completely fill the medium cup? Two — how many small cups of water will completely fill the large cup? Do not discuss yet. You have 60 seconds.' [WAIT 60 seconds in silence.] Then say: 'Now turn to your shoulder partner and compare your answers. You have 30 seconds.' [WAIT 30 seconds.] Cold-call 6 learners (aim for a spread of predictions): 'Amina, what did you write for the medium cup?' — 'Brian, do you agree or disagree with Amina, and why?' — repeat for 4 more learners. Record all unique prediction values on the board under the heading PREDICTIONS — DO NOT ERASE. Do not confirm or deny any prediction. Say: 'We are going to test these predictions right now. Keep your sticky note — you will need it later.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-before-you-observe (Anchored Prediction): Requiring a written, committed prediction before evidence is seen forces learners to make their current mental model explicit. When evidence later contradicts the prediction, cognitive conflict is maximised because every learner has a personal stake in the discrepancy. Recording all predictions publicly on the board validates all thinking and communicates that the goal is sense-making, not being correct.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans sticky notes as learners write. Look for: (a) whether learners predict 2 and 3 (linear scaling — the expected misconception), (b) whether any learner predicts 4 and 9 (correct — note for later discussion), (c) whether learners give non-integer answers (shows proportional reasoning). The distribution of predictions reveals the class's prior understanding of scaling and flags the misconception to address explicitly in the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher fills the small cup with water and pours it into the medium cup, counting aloud with the class. Learners observe and tally on a mini-observation table in their notebooks: Cup pair | Predicted fills | Actual fills | Surprised? (Y/N). The teacher repeats for the large cup. Learners then move into groups of four and collect 4–6 everyday objects from around the room and their bags. Using rulers, they measure the length and width of corresponding faces of pairs of objects they believe are similar and record results in a measurement table: Object A length | Object A width | Object B length | Object B width | Ratio L(B)/L(A) | Ratio W(B)/W(A). Groups also compare corresponding angles using the corner of a sheet of paper as a right-angle checker.
framework.teacherMoves: Hold up the small cup. Say: 'I am going to fill this small cup with water and pour it into the medium cup. Everyone count with me — out loud — each time I pour.' Fill and pour. Count with the class. After the fourth pour fills the medium cup say: 'Four. Not two.' [Pause 15 seconds — do not explain, allow silence and reactions.] Then say: 'Now let us do the large cup.' Repeat pouring from the small cup into the large cup, counting to nine. Say: 'Nine. Not three. Your predictions are on the board. Look at them.' [Pause 10 seconds.] Say: 'In your notebook, complete the observation table I have written on the board. Then write one sentence beginning: I am surprised because…' [WAIT 90 seconds.] Cold-call 3 learners to read their sentence. Then say: 'Hold on to that surprise — it is the question that will drive this entire unit.' Transition to group activity: 'Now I want each group to collect objects from around you — tin cans, boxes, books, anything with a clear rectangular or circular face. Pick pairs you think look similar — same shape, different size. Measure them. I will come around.' Circulate to all groups within 8 minutes. At each group ask: 'What ratio did you get for the lengths? What ratio for the widths? Are they the same or different?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discrepant Event followed by Structured Data Collection: The live pouring demonstration creates a discrepant event — an observable outcome that violates a strongly held prediction. The follow-up measurement activity shifts learners from passive surprise to active evidence-gathering, channelling the cognitive conflict into a structured search for pattern. Recording ratios in a two-column table (ratio of lengths vs. ratio of widths) makes the constancy of the ratio visible as data, not just assertion.
framework.formativeAssessment: During group measurement, the teacher checks: (a) Are learners measuring corresponding sides (length-to-length, width-to-width) or mixing dimensions? (b) Are calculated ratios consistent within a pair (both ≈ 2.0, or both ≈ 1.5)? (c) Can a learner in the group articulate verbally why constant ratios matter? A group that has inconsistent ratios has likely picked a non-similar pair — use this as a teaching moment: 'Are you sure these two shapes are the same shape?' Groups that finish early are prompted: 'Now check the angles at each corner — are they equal?'

framework.learnerExperience: Each group shares one pair of objects they measured and their ratio results. The class collates findings on a shared class table on the board. Learners identify that for all pairs they agreed were 'similar,' the ratio of corresponding lengths was constant and the corresponding angles were equal. The teacher formalises these two properties and introduces the term linear scale factor. Learners write the formal definition in their notebooks and label a diagram of two similar rectangles with the scale factor. They connect this back to the uji cups: the cups have a linear scale factor of 2 (medium:small), yet the water fills were 4 — a number the teacher asks learners to notice equals 2².
framework.teacherMoves: Bring the class back together. Say: 'Each group, give me one sentence: what ratio did you find, and do you think your two objects are similar?' Cold-call all 6 groups in turn. Record each group's ratio on the board class table. Say: 'Look at this table. What do you notice about the groups whose objects you all agree look similar?' [WAIT 15 seconds.] Invite 3 learners: 'Zawadi, what do you see?' After responses, say: 'The pattern you have found has a name. When two figures are similar, their corresponding angles are equal AND the ratios of their corresponding sides are equal. That constant ratio is called the LINEAR SCALE FACTOR — we write it as k.' Write on the board: Similar figures → (1) Corresponding angles equal, (2) Corresponding sides in constant ratio k. Say: 'Now look at the uji cups. The medium cup has a linear scale factor of k = 2 compared to the small cup. We filled it with 4 small cups of water. Someone tell me: what is 2 squared?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Cold-call 2 learners. Say: 'And the large cup: k = 3, fills = 9. What is 3 squared?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Say: 'Write this in your notebook and circle it: k = 2 → fills = 4 = 2². k = 3 → fills = 9 = 3². We are not ready to explain this fully yet — but keep it in mind. That is our puzzle for the unit.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Class Data Synthesis with Formal Definition Anchoring: Pooling group measurements into a single class table makes the pattern (constant ratio = similar) emerge from the learners' own data rather than being imposed by the teacher. Formal vocabulary is introduced only after the pattern is visible in the data, so the definition is a name for something learners have already noticed. Connecting the formal definition immediately back to the phenomenon (k = 2, fills = 4 = k²) plants the seed of the area-scale-factor relationship without requiring learners to explain it yet.
framework.formativeAssessment: Exit check: ask learners to quickly sketch two rectangles where one has sides 3 cm × 2 cm and the other has sides 6 cm × 4 cm, and write whether they are similar and what the linear scale factor is. Circulate and check: (a) Does the learner correctly identify k = 2? (b) Does the learner correctly identify that angles are equal (all 90°)? (c) Does the learner check both ratios (6/3 = 2 AND 4/2 = 2)? This takes 2 minutes and reveals whether the formal definition has been internalised before the DQB phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes one question on a sticky note prompted by what they observed or cannot yet explain — especially about the uji cup mystery. Sticky notes are posted on a dedicated section of the wall or board labelled DRIVING QUESTION BOARD. The teacher reads selected questions aloud and the class organises them into two columns: Things we have noticed and Things we still cannot explain. The central driving question — 'Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much?' — is written in large text at the top of the DQB by the teacher if not already suggested by a learner.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute a new sticky note to each learner. Say: 'Think about everything you saw and measured today. Write one question — something you observed that you cannot yet explain, or something you want to understand by the end of this unit. Start your question with WHY, HOW, or WHAT IF.' [WAIT 2 minutes in silence.] Then say: 'Come and post your question on the board.' Once all notes are posted, read 5–6 aloud, grouping similar questions by placing them close together. Say: 'I notice many of you are asking about the water cups — why four, why nine. That is our central mystery.' Write on the board in large letters: DRIVING QUESTION — Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much — and how can we use this pattern to design and predict the properties of any similar shape? Say: 'Every lesson this unit, we will come back to this board. As we answer questions, we will move them to the EXPLAINED side. Questions that are still open stay here. By the end of the unit, this board should be mostly on the EXPLAINED side.' Point to the two columns you have labelled: STILL WONDERING | WE CAN NOW EXPLAIN.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB) — Public Knowledge Tracker: The DQB makes the class's collective knowledge state visible and persistent. It externalises metacognition: learners can see what the class knows and what remains mysterious. Returning to the DQB at the start and end of every lesson creates a storyline thread — learners experience their own growing understanding as a narrative, not as isolated facts. Anchoring the DQB to the phenomenon ensures that abstract mathematical learning is always connected to a concrete, memorable context.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all sticky notes before the next lesson and categorises them: (a) questions about area scaling (k²) — will be addressed in Lesson 3; (b) questions about volume scaling (k³) — will be addressed in Lesson 5; (c) questions about what 'corresponding' means — address in Lesson 2 warm-up; (d) questions that reveal a continuing misconception (e.g. 'Is k = 2 because the cup is twice as tall?') — flag for explicit address in Lesson 2. This informs the teacher's planning for subsequent lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: In their notebooks, learners draw and label their first unit model: two similar rectangles (one with sides 3 cm × 2 cm, one with sides 6 cm × 4 cm), annotated with arrows showing corresponding sides, the ratio calculation written beside each pair of corresponding sides, and k = 2 written prominently. Below the rectangles, learners sketch the three uji cups (labelled small, medium, large) and write the linear scale factors k = 2 and k = 3 beside the medium and large cups. They leave a blank box labelled '? fills' under each cup — to be completed in a future lesson when they understand why fills = k².
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'In your notebook, on a fresh page, draw your first model for this unit. It has two parts. Part one: draw two similar rectangles — the small one is 3 cm by 2 cm. Use your ruler. The large one has k = 2. Draw it beside the small one. Label the sides. Write the ratio calculation. Part two: below the rectangles, sketch the three uji cups — label them small, medium, large. Write k = 2 beside the medium cup and k = 3 beside the large cup. Leave a blank box under each cup and write inside it: ? — we will fill this in as we learn more.' Circulate for 4 minutes. Check that learners: (a) have drawn the large rectangle with sides 6 cm × 4 cm (not 5 cm × 4 cm or other), (b) have written ratio calculations, (c) have k correctly labelled. Say: 'This model is the beginning. Every lesson we will add to it. By the end of the unit it will explain everything on the Driving Question Board.' Cold-call one learner to hold up their model and describe it to the class in one sentence.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Annotated Model (CAM): Requiring learners to build a single evolving model — rather than isolated diagrams per lesson — creates a physical representation of the unit storyline in every learner's notebook. The deliberate blank boxes ('? fills') embed the unresolved mystery directly into the model, so that the mathematical tension is visible and persistent. Each time a blank is filled in a future lesson, learners experience a concrete sense of progress and explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher does a rapid gallery walk during the 4-minute drawing period. Look for: (a) correct second rectangle dimensions (6 × 4); (b) ratio written as a fraction or decimal beside each pair of sides; (c) k = 2 and k = 3 labels on the cup sketches. Learners who have the wrong second rectangle dimensions (common error: adding 2 to each side instead of multiplying) are asked: 'You found k = 2 from the data. How did you get k = 2 from 3 cm to your new length?' This probes multiplicative vs. additive thinking — the most critical prerequisite misconception for the unit.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. When learners saw that the medium cup needed 4 small cups of water (not 2), how did they react — surprise, disengagement, or immediate curiosity? Did the discrepant event generate the cognitive conflict you hoped for, and if not, how could you strengthen the setup (e.g. asking learners to bet on their prediction before pouring)?

2. During the group measurement activity, did most groups correctly identify similar pairs and find consistent ratios for both length and width? Which groups struggled, and was the difficulty conceptual (not understanding what 'corresponding' means) or procedural (inaccurate measuring technique)?

3. When you cold-called learners to share their DQB questions, did the questions reveal understanding of the area/volume scaling mystery, or were most questions about the definition of similarity itself? What does this tell you about the level at which to pitch Lesson 2?

4. In the Model Building phase, how many learners made the additive error (adding k to each dimension instead of multiplying)? This misconception — that scaling is additive — is the root cause of all later errors in this unit. Plan a specific 5-minute warm-up for Lesson 2 to address it if more than a quarter of the class made this error.

5. Did the three uji cups feel authentic and culturally relevant to learners, or did the context feel contrived? Could you involve learners in bringing similar-shaped containers from home for Lesson 2 to increase ownership and relevance of the phenomenon?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Three uji cups of different sizes (small, medium, large) share the same shape — every dimension of the medium cup is exactly twice that of the small cup (k = 2) and every dimension of the large cup is exactly three times that of the small cup (k = 3). When filled with water, the medium cup required 4 small cups (not 2) and the large cup required 9 small cups (not 3). In everyday objects measured by groups, similar pairs showed equal corresponding angles and a constant ratio of corresponding sides.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Two figures are similar if and only if their corresponding angles are equal AND their corresponding sides are in a constant ratio called the linear scale factor (k). Similarity is about shape, not size. The linear scale factor k can be found by dividing the length of any side of the larger figure by the corresponding side of the smaller figure. For the uji cups, k = 2 (medium:small) and k = 3 (large:small) — but the number of water fills was k² = 4 and k² = 9, not k itself. This k² pattern is the mystery that the rest of the unit will explain.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The three uji cups are similar solids — they share the same shape, with all dimensions scaled by the same factor k. This is why they look proportional to the eye. However, the amount of water each holds (related to cross-sectional area and volume) does not scale by k but by a larger power of k. Today's lesson establishes the foundation — the definition of similarity and the meaning of k — which is the first step toward building a mathematical model that predicts the 'surprising' water-fill numbers and explains why scaling lengths by k scales areas and volumes by higher powers of k.

LESSONS.title: Centre of Enlargement and Linear Scale Factor

slo.purpose: Learners investigate how enlargement works by physically locating the centre of enlargement and computing the linear scale factor from real traced figures, building the mathematical foundation needed to later explain why the uji cups hold 4× and 9× as much water.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know: (a) what the centre of enlargement is and how to locate it by drawing lines through corresponding vertices; (b) how to measure corresponding sides of an object and its image; (c) how to calculate the linear scale factor k = image length ÷ object length.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) trace an object and its image on plain paper and locate the centre of enlargement; (b) measure corresponding sides accurately using a ruler; (c) compute the linear scale factor k from at least three pairs of corresponding sides; (d) draw the image of a simple polygon given a centre of enlargement and a linear scale factor.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that enlargement is a precise, rule-governed transformation — not a freehand 'making bigger' — and will develop confidence in using geometric tools to uncover mathematical structure hidden in everyday objects such as the uji cups.
slo.keyInquiry: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners noticed the puzzling water-filling results with the uji cups and asked: 'What rule controls how the cups scale?' Lesson 2 answers the first part of that question by revealing the geometric engine behind enlargement — the centre of enlargement and the linear scale factor k. Once learners see that every ray from the centre passes through both the object vertex and the image vertex, and that k tells us exactly how far each point moves, they have the conceptual tool to later explain why area scales as k² and volume as k³.
slo.safetyNotes: No significant hazards. Remind learners to handle drawing compasses and sharp pencils carefully. Ensure tables are clear of bags to avoid tripping when learners move to compare traced figures.

LESSONS.overview: Learners open by revisiting the uji cup mystery from Lesson 1 and predicting what geometric rule might control how the cups were made 'the same shape but different size.' They then carry out a hands-on tracing activity: each pair traces a simple polygon (a cut-out of a Kenyan chai cup cross-section) and its pre-drawn enlarged image, then draws rays through corresponding vertices to pinpoint the centre of enlargement. They measure at least three pairs of corresponding sides and compute k each time, discovering that k is constant for all pairs. A second example with a different object (a Rift Valley tea-leaf outline) placed at a different centre consolidates the concept. Learners close by updating the Driving Question Board and beginning a cumulative anchor model linking k to the cup phenomenon.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a half-page printed sheet showing two similar triangles — labelled 'Small Uji Cup profile' and 'Large Uji Cup profile' — placed on plain paper with no centre marked. Learners individually write responses to two prompts in their exercise books: (1) 'How do you think the manufacturer moved every point of the small cup outward to create the large cup? Draw an arrow showing your idea.' (2) 'If the large cup's height is 12 cm and the small cup's height is 4 cm, predict what single number describes the relationship between every pair of matching lengths.' Learners share predictions with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the printed sheet face-down. Say: 'Do NOT flip it over yet.' After 30 seconds of silence, say: 'Flip and read — you have 3 minutes to write your own prediction before talking to anyone.' [WAIT — 3 minutes individual silent writing.] Then say: 'Now share your prediction with your partner. You have 2 minutes. I want to hear the number you predicted AND the reason.' Circulate and listen; note 2–3 varied predictions on a sticky note for later reference. After partner talk, cold-call 3 learners (choose one who predicted k = 3, one who predicted k = 2, one who is uncertain): 'Amina, what number did you predict and why?' [WAIT 10 seconds after each nomination before accepting response.] Record all three predictions visibly on the board under the heading 'OUR PREDICTIONS — we will check these today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with Anchored Prediction: by requiring learners to commit a number and a reason to paper before discussion, the teacher activates prior knowledge from Lesson 1 (the cup measurements) and creates cognitive dissonance that the Observe phase will resolve. Recording predictions publicly creates accountability and gives the teacher formative data about misconceptions (e.g., learners who think the number is 2 because 'it looks twice as big').
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learner has written a specific numerical prediction (not 'bigger') AND a geometric reason (e.g., 'rays go out from a point,' 'everything moves the same amount'). Teacher notes which learners write only a number with no geometric reasoning — these learners need targeted questioning during the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: ACTIVITY A — Locating the Centre (15 min): Each pair receives: one A4 plain paper sheet with a pre-drawn pentagon labelled ABCDE (object, side ≈ 3 cm) and its enlarged image A'B'C'D'E' already printed, positioned so the centre of enlargement is on the page but unmarked; one ruler; one sharp pencil. Pairs draw a straight line through A and A', extending it in both directions. They repeat for B→B' and C→C'. They mark the point where all three lines meet and label it O — the centre of enlargement. Learners measure OA and OA', then OB and OB', then OC and OC'. They record the six measurements in a table and compute the ratio OA'/OA, OB'/OB, OC'/OC for each pair. ACTIVITY B — Computing k from Side Lengths (10 min): Pairs now measure corresponding sides: A'B'/AB, B'C'/BC, C'D'/CD, D'E'/DE, E'A'/EA. They record all five ratios in a second table. They write a sentence: 'The linear scale factor k = ___ because every ratio of image side to object side equals ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Before releasing materials say: 'You are now the manufacturer's quality inspector. Your job is to prove — using your ruler and straight lines — exactly where the factory's enlargement machine was centred. This is the secret behind how every uji cup in Kenya is made identical in shape.' Distribute materials. [WAIT — allow 2 minutes for pairs to attempt drawing rays before intervening.] Circulate; for any pair drawing rays that do not converge, crouch to their level and ask: 'Are you drawing through BOTH the object vertex AND the image vertex? Check your pencil is on A first, then slide it to A'.' Do NOT draw the line for them — guide only. After 8 minutes, pause the class: 'Raise your hand if your three lines all meet at one point.' [Count hands aloud.] 'Excellent — Kariuki's group and Fatuma's group, what do you notice about where O landed relative to the two pentagons?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Cold-call 2 more groups. For Activity B, say: 'Now use your ruler — not your eye — to measure EVERY pair of matching sides. Record every measurement. I will be checking that you have at least five ratios in your table.' Circulate and check tables. If a ratio differs from the others by more than 0.1, prompt: 'Re-measure that side — start your ruler exactly at the vertex.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Hands-On Data Collection with Ratio Table: learners generate their own numerical evidence rather than being told k. The repeated act of measuring five different pairs and obtaining the same ratio each time creates the 'aha' that k is a property of the whole transformation, not just one pair of sides. This directly mirrors how the uji cup manufacturer would verify that every dimension scaled identically.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Three rays drawn through corresponding vertex pairs that visibly converge at a single point O. (2) A completed two-column ratio table with at least five entries, all values within ±0.1 of each other. (3) A written sentence correctly identifying k as a constant ratio. Teacher flags any pair whose ratios vary by more than 0.2 for immediate re-measurement support.

framework.learnerExperience: CONSOLIDATION EXAMPLE (8 min): Each learner individually draws the image of a simple quadrilateral PQRS (given on a printed grid, side lengths 2 cm each, forming a square) under an enlargement with centre O (marked at a specific grid point) and scale factor k = 3. Learners must: (a) draw a ray from O through P and mark P' at distance OP × 3 from O; (b) repeat for Q, R, S; (c) join P'Q'R'S'; (d) verify by measuring one pair of sides. DISCUSSION (12 min): Whole-class structured discussion using the displayed anchor photograph of the three uji cups. Teacher writes on the board: 'Small cup height = 5 cm. Medium cup height = 10 cm. Large cup height = 15 cm. Where is the centre of enlargement for the cup manufacturer?' Learners discuss in groups of 4 for 3 minutes, then share. Teacher records key agreed statements: 'k from small to medium = ___'; 'k from small to large = ___'; 'Every length on the medium cup is ___ times the matching length on the small cup.'
framework.teacherMoves: For the individual drawing task, say: 'Close your books. No partner help for 8 minutes. This is your chance to show me YOU can do this.' [WAIT — enforce individual silence.] Circulate and observe; mark a small tick in pencil next to any correctly placed image vertex. After 8 minutes say: 'Swap books with your partner. Check each other's P', Q', R', S' using your ruler. If a point is more than 2 mm off, mark it with a question mark — do not erase your partner's work.' [WAIT 2 minutes.] Open the whole-class discussion by displaying the uji cup photo. Ask: 'Baraka, if you were standing at the centre of enlargement, what would you see?' [WAIT 12 seconds — this is deliberately open.] Then: 'Adhiambo, how does the scale factor k we measured today help explain why the manufacturer can guarantee every cup is the same shape?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Cold-call one more learner: 'Mwangi, complete this sentence on the board for us: The linear scale factor k tells us that every length on the image is ___.' Correct any statement that says 'k tells us the size' — redirect: 'k tells us the RATIO of lengths, not the actual size. Say it again using the word ratio.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Individual Application followed by Peer Verification and Whole-Class Anchoring: the individual drawing task forces each learner to operationalise the procedure (not just observe it). Peer verification builds checking habits. The return to the uji cup anchors the abstract procedure in the phenomenon, ensuring the Explain phase does not float free of the unit's driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Correctly constructed image P'Q'R'S' with all four vertices within 2 mm of correct position, confirmed by peer check. (2) During discussion, learner can state k numerically (k = 2 for small→medium, k = 3 for small→large) unprompted. (3) Learner's written sentence uses the word 'ratio' or 'times' rather than 'size' or 'bigger.' Teacher notes any learner who cannot place even one image vertex correctly — schedule one-on-one support before Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner takes two sticky notes. On the GREEN note they write one thing they NOW KNOW that they did not know at the start of today's lesson (must include the word 'centre' or 'k'). On the ORANGE note they write one new question that today's lesson raised for them — ideally connecting to the driving question about the cups. Learners post both notes on the class DQB under the columns 'NOW WE KNOW' and 'WE STILL WONDER.' The class reads the orange notes aloud in a 2-minute gallery walk around the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You have 3 minutes — individual, silent writing on your sticky notes. The green note must have the word CENTRE or K in it. The orange note must connect to our uji cups.' [Enforce 3-minute silence.] After posting, lead a 2-minute gallery walk: 'Walk around — read every orange question — put a small dot on any question that is ALSO in your head.' After the walk, identify the 2–3 most-dotted orange questions and read them aloud: 'These are our class's best wondering questions. Let's read them: [read]. Baraza ya darasa — class parliament — does anyone want to make a prediction about the answer? We will keep these questions up and see if we can answer them by Lesson 4.' Do NOT answer the questions now; validate them: 'These are exactly the kind of questions mathematicians ask.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB as Living Document: the DQB is not a one-time poster but a running record of the class's evolving understanding. Requiring the word 'centre' or 'k' on the green note prevents vague entries ('I learned about enlargement') and ensures metacognitive specificity. The dot-voting on orange notes surfaces the most broadly felt uncertainties, which the teacher uses to sequence Lessons 3–5.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Green note contains a specific, accurate statement referencing 'centre of enlargement' or 'k = image/object.' (2) Orange note poses a question that goes beyond today's content (e.g., 'Does k affect how much water the cup holds?' or 'What happens to the area if k = 3?'). Teacher photographs the DQB after class to track conceptual progression across the unit.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their 'Anchor Model' page — a running diagram they began in Lesson 1 showing the three uji cups side by side with their measurements. Today they ADD to the diagram: (a) they draw a dot labelled O above or to the left of the cups and draw rays from O through the top-rim of the small cup extending to the top-rim of the medium and large cups; (b) they label the scale factors k = 2 (small→medium) and k = 3 (small→large) on the rays; (c) they write in a box beside the diagram: 'Linear scale factor k = image length ÷ object length. For the uji cups: k² = ??? and k³ = ???' — the ??? boxes are deliberately left blank to be filled in Lesson 3. Learners share their updated model with their partner and agree on the placement of O and the labels.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Turn to your Anchor Model page. Today we are adding the mathematical engine — the centre and the scale factor. You have 8 minutes to update your diagram. The two ??? boxes should stay blank — they are your questions for Lesson 3.' [WAIT — 8 minutes working time.] Circulate and check: (a) Is O outside both cup shapes? (b) Do the rays pass through corresponding points on both cups? (c) Are k = 2 and k = 3 labelled on the correct rays? For any model where O is placed BETWEEN the cups, ask: 'If O is between the cups, which direction would you travel from O to reach the small cup, and which direction to reach the large cup? Can that be right?' After 8 minutes: 'Show your partner your model. If your partner's O is in a different position from yours, discuss for 1 minute and agree on the correct position before we close.' Cold-call one pair to describe their model to the class in 30 seconds. Close with: 'Next lesson we will fill in those ??? boxes — and you will see why the answer is NOT 2 and NOT 3, and why that is the secret the uji cups have been hiding.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision with Intentional Incompleteness: the ??? boxes are a deliberate instructional move — they make the model's incompleteness visible and motivating, directly sustaining the cognitive tension from the phenomenon. By requiring learners to draw O and the rays onto the cup diagram, the teacher ensures that the abstract geometric concept (centre of enlargement) is physically integrated into the anchoring phenomenon rather than existing as a separate textbook procedure.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) O is placed outside both cup profiles, with rays correctly extending through corresponding points on each cup. (2) k = 2 and k = 3 are correctly labelled on the appropriate rays (small→medium and small→large respectively). (3) The two ??? boxes are present and blank — confirming the learner recognises the model is incomplete. Teacher collects 5 randomly selected Anchor Model pages to review before Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) How many learners successfully located the centre of enlargement independently (rays converging at one point) without teacher redirection? If fewer than 70% succeeded unaided, plan a 5-minute re-teach at the start of Lesson 3 using a different pair of similar shapes. (2) Which orange DQB questions most frequently appeared? If learners are already asking about area or volume, you can foreground those connections earlier in Lesson 3. (3) Did any learner's ratio table show significantly inconsistent values (e.g., ratios ranging from 1.8 to 3.1)? This signals a ruler-reading or measurement skill gap — address individually before the assessment task. (4) Were the uji cup connections made explicitly by learners, or only by the teacher? If learners are not yet volunteering the cup connection, increase the frequency of explicit anchoring prompts in Lessons 3 and 4.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners traced a pentagon ABCDE and its enlarged image on plain paper, drew rays through three pairs of corresponding vertices (A→A', B→B', C→C'), and identified the single point O where all rays intersected as the centre of enlargement. They also measured five pairs of corresponding sides on the pentagon and computed the ratio image÷object for each pair.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The centre of enlargement O is the unique fixed point from which every vertex of the object is projected outward to its corresponding image vertex. The linear scale factor k = image length ÷ object length is constant for ALL pairs of corresponding lengths in an enlargement — it does not vary from side to side. For the uji cups, k = 2 (small→medium) and k = 3 (small→large), meaning every single length on the medium cup is exactly twice the matching length on the small cup.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Because k is the ratio of ANY matching pair of lengths, the manufacturer can guarantee that the large uji cup is geometrically similar to the small one simply by using the same centre of enlargement and the same scale factor k for every point. This is why the cups 'look the same' despite being different sizes. However, k only describes lengths — the class has not yet explained why filling the cup requires k² times as much water in cross-section, or k³ times as much in volume. Those ??? boxes in the Anchor Model will be resolved in Lesson 3.
