LESSONS.title: Drawing Enlargements — Constructing Images from a Centre and Scale Factor
LESSONS.aresKeywords: centre of enlargement, linear scale factor, image construction, similar figures, enlargement drawing

slo.purpose: Learners construct the image of a given figure using a centre of enlargement and a linear scale factor (k = 2, 3, and ½), then verify by measurement that all lengths scale by k while all angles remain unchanged — directly connecting the uji cup k-pattern to a precise geometric construction procedure.
slo.knowledge:
• The image of each vertex is found by drawing a ray from the centre of enlargement O through the object vertex and measuring k times the object distance along that ray.
• Under enlargement by scale factor k, every length in the image is exactly k times the corresponding object length, but every angle remains equal to its corresponding object angle.
• A scale factor k > 1 produces an enlargement (image larger than object); 0 < k < 1 produces a reduction (image smaller than object); k = 1 leaves the figure unchanged.
slo.skills:
• Accurately construct the image of a given polygon given a centre of enlargement and a linear scale factor using a ruler and straight edge.
• Verify an enlargement construction by measuring corresponding lengths and confirming the ratio equals k, and by measuring corresponding angles and confirming they are equal.
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate the precision required in geometric construction and the satisfaction of a verified result.
• Recognise that the mathematical pattern discovered in the uji cup phenomenon (scaling by k) is not accidental — it is a necessary consequence of how enlargement works.
slo.keyInquiry: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1 and 2 established what similarity means and where the centre of enlargement is. This lesson translates that understanding into action: learners now construct enlargements themselves, confirm that every length scales by k while every angle is preserved, and begin to see WHY the uji cup areas came out as k² — because both dimensions of the cup's cross-section scaled by k simultaneously.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners use rulers and pencils with sharp points. Remind learners to keep compass/pencil points directed downward and away from peers when passing materials. No other specific hazards.

LESSONS.overview:
In this third lesson of the evidence-gathering sequence, learners move from recognising and measuring similarity (Lessons 1–2) to actively constructing it. Each learner draws the image of a simple polygon — first a triangle, then a rectangle — given a printed centre of enlargement O and a stated linear scale factor. They work with k = 2, k = 3, and k = ½ in turn, mirroring the exact ratios found on the uji cups (small→medium and small→large). After constructing each image, learners measure every pair of corresponding sides and confirm the ratio equals k, then use a protractor to confirm every pair of corresponding angles is equal. This measurement-verification step is the core evidence-gathering activity of the lesson.

The lesson is anchored throughout in Kenyan real-life contexts: a photographer in Mombasa who must enlarge a portrait to poster size for a political rally (k = 3), and a cartographer at the Survey of Kenya who scales a detailed street map of Kisumu down to fit a regional atlas page (k = ½). These contexts frame the central question — what changes and what stays the same? — and lead learners to articulate the fundamental result: enlargement preserves shape (angles) but changes size (lengths). This distinction is then connected back to the uji cups: the cups are enlargements of one another, so every length on the medium cup is exactly twice (k = 2) the matching length on the small cup, and this is why the cross-sectional area came out four times — both the diameter and the height scaled by 2 at the same time.

By the close of the lesson, learners update their Driving Question Board with two new claims: (1) construction gives us a precise tool for predicting where the image of any point will land, and (2) angles are invariant under enlargement, but lengths are not — they scale by k. These claims directly advance the driving question by explaining the mechanism behind the uji cup mystery and setting up Lesson 4's investigation of area scale factor (k²).

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a half-sheet showing a small triangle ABC printed on plain paper, with a point O clearly marked 4 cm to the left of vertex A. Before touching a ruler, learners individually sketch — in pencil, on the same sheet — where they think the image triangle A′B′C′ will appear if the figure is enlarged by k = 2 from centre O. They annotate their sketch with a sentence: 'I think the image will be [larger/smaller/same size] because…' and a second sentence predicting whether the angles will change. Learners then share predictions with a shoulder partner for 60 seconds.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the predict sheets face-down. Say: 'Do NOT turn over until I say go. You are going to predict — not calculate, not construct — just sketch your best guess.' After 90 seconds of individual silent sketching, say: 'Tell your partner two things: where you drew the image, and whether you think the angles will stay the same or change. You have 60 seconds — go.' After partner talk, cold-call 3 learners (choose one confident, one hesitant, one who looks uncertain): 'Akinyi, where did you draw your image — farther from O or closer?' — WAIT 10 seconds. 'Omondi, same or different angles?' — WAIT 10 seconds. 'Fatuma, do you agree with Omondi — why or why not?' — WAIT 12 seconds. Record the three prediction positions on the board as quick sketches labelled P1, P2, P3. Say: 'We will come back to these predictions at the end of the Observe phase and see who was closest — and more importantly, WHY.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction Sketching with Annotated Reasoning — learners externalise their mental model of enlargement before instruction. By committing to a sketch and a written sentence, they activate prior knowledge from Lessons 1–2 (centre of enlargement, k as a ratio) and create a cognitive anchor. The subsequent partner share surfaces misconceptions (e.g., 'the image just slides to the right' or 'angles get bigger too') that the teacher can target during the Observe phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans the room during sketching and looks for: (1) learners who place the image on the opposite side of O from the object — a sign they are confusing enlargement with reflection; (2) learners who draw an image the same size as the object — indicating k = 2 has not been internalised; (3) learners who correctly place the image farther from O and larger. Teacher notes these three groups mentally to differentiate cold-call questions in the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in pairs to perform three timed construction tasks on pre-printed worksheets, each showing an object figure, a marked centre O, and a stated scale factor. Task 1: Enlarge triangle PQR by k = 2 from centre O (mimicking the small-to-medium uji cup). Task 2: Enlarge the same triangle by k = 3 from the same O (small-to-large cup). Task 3: Reduce rectangle ABCD by k = ½ from O (mimicking the cartographer in Kisumu shrinking a map). For each task, learners use the step-by-step construction protocol written on the board: (a) Draw a ray from O through each vertex. (b) Measure the distance from O to the vertex. (c) Multiply by k and mark the image vertex on the ray at that distance. (d) Connect image vertices to form the image figure. After constructing, they fill in a verification table: measure each pair of corresponding sides and compute the ratio; measure each pair of corresponding angles and record.
framework.teacherMoves: Write the four-step construction protocol on the board before distributing worksheets. Read each step aloud and mime the ruler action. Say: 'Step 1 — ray from O through the vertex. Step 2 — measure O to vertex. Step 3 — multiply by k, mark the new point. Step 4 — join the new points. Simple. Let us do Task 1 together for just the first vertex P, then you continue.' Demonstrate on a large printed copy taped to the board: measure OP aloud ('I measure 3 cm'), multiply ('3 × 2 = 6 cm'), mark P′ ('I mark 6 cm from O along the ray'). Say: 'Now you do vertices Q and R and connect P′Q′R′. You have 4 minutes.' Circulate — at the 2-minute mark, cold-call one pair: 'Show me your ray for vertex Q — is Q′ farther from O or closer than Q?' — WAIT 10 seconds. After Task 1, pause the class: 'Check your verification table — what ratio did you get for side P′Q′ ÷ PQ? Raise your hand if you got exactly 2.' Scan room. 'What about the angle at Q′ compared to Q?' Cold-call 2 pairs. Repeat the pause-and-check after Tasks 2 and 3. Connect to context: 'This is exactly what a photographer in Mombasa does when blowing up a portrait to poster size — every length triples, but Uncle Kamau's face still looks like Uncle Kamau because the angles stay the same.' For Task 3, ask: 'The cartographer at Survey of Kenya uses k = ½ — what happens to the distances from O?' — WAIT 12 seconds — cold-call 2 learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Construction with Immediate Measurement Verification — the four-step protocol makes the abstract definition of enlargement (image distance = k × object distance from O) into a concrete, repeatable physical procedure. The verification table forces learners to generate their own quantitative evidence that lengths scale by k and angles do not. This is the same evidence-gathering logic used in Lesson 1 when learners measured the uji cups: observe → measure → compute ratio → draw conclusion.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks verification tables during circulation. Success indicators: (a) all three side-length ratios in the table equal k (within ±0.1 cm measurement tolerance); (b) all three angle measurements in the table show equality between object and image (within ±2°). Red-flag indicators: any ratio that is not k suggests the learner measured from the vertex rather than from O; any angle discrepancy greater than 5° suggests incorrect image vertex placement. Teacher notes pairs with errors for targeted support during the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: The class reconvenes. Each pair writes three statements on a sticky note (or speaks aloud if sticky notes are unavailable): (1) 'Under enlargement by k, lengths [increase/decrease/stay the same] by a factor of ___.' (2) 'Under enlargement by k, angles [increase/decrease/stay the same].' (3) 'The centre of enlargement O [does/does not] change position.' Pairs share their statements. The teacher then poses the critical connection question: 'Think back to the uji cups. The medium cup had k = 2 compared to the small cup. Its height was 2× and its diameter was 2×. If I want to know the area of the circular top of the medium cup compared to the small cup — I am scaling TWO lengths each by 2. What do you think happens to the area?' Learners discuss in pairs for 90 seconds, then the class works through the reasoning together: Area = π × r². If r is doubled (k = 2), new area = π × (2r)² = 4πr² = 4 × original area. The teacher writes k² = 4 on the board and links it to the 4 small cups of water needed to fill the medium uji cup from Lesson 1.
framework.teacherMoves: After collecting sticky notes, read out three contrasting responses (one correct, one partially correct, one with a misconception about angles). Do NOT say which is right yet — say: 'Three different ideas on the board — let us use our verification tables to decide.' Cold-call the pair whose verification table showed the clearest evidence: 'Read me your angle column for Task 1.' — WAIT 10 seconds. After confirmation, write the three conclusions on the board in learner-friendly language: 'LENGTHS: multiply by k. ANGLES: stay the same. CENTRE O: stays put.' Then say: 'Now here is the big connection. Pause and think: the uji cup phenomenon — why did the medium cup need FOUR small cups of water to fill the circular cross-section, not two? Talk to your partner. I will ask in 90 seconds.' — WAIT the full 90 seconds. Cold-call 3 pairs in sequence, building the argument incrementally: 'Wanjiku, what is the radius of the medium cup compared to the small one?' — WAIT 10 seconds. 'Kipchoge, so what is the area of the circular top of the medium cup?' — WAIT 12 seconds. 'Amina, does that match what we found in Lesson 1 with the water fills?' — WAIT 10 seconds. Write on the board: 'k = 2 → k² = 4 (area). k = 3 → k² = 9 (area).' Circle both numbers and draw an arrow to the uji cup diagram on the wall.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) Protocol — learners construct explicit written claims ('lengths multiply by k'), identify the evidence from their verification tables (measured ratios), and begin to reason toward the k² result for area. This bridges the procedural skill of construction (Observe phase) to the conceptual understanding of why areas scale as k². The teacher's Socratic cold-call sequence scaffolds the reasoning step-by-step rather than simply telling learners the answer.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher listens to pair discussions during the 90-second think time. Success indicators: learners spontaneously use the phrase 'both dimensions scale by k' or write Area = (kr)². Misconception to watch for: learners saying 'area doubles because k = 2' — this shows they are adding k rather than squaring it. If this misconception surfaces, the teacher draws a 1 cm × 1 cm square, then a 2 cm × 2 cm square, and asks: 'How many small squares fit inside the big one?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board (a large sheet of paper or section of the chalkboard divided into three columns: QUESTIONS | WHAT WE KNOW | WHAT WE THINK). Each pair writes one new 'WHAT WE KNOW' sticky note from today's lesson and one new 'QUESTION' that today's lesson has raised. Suggested sentence starters are displayed: 'We now know that…' and 'We still wonder…'. Pairs stick their notes in the correct columns. The teacher reads selected entries aloud and the class votes (thumbs up/sideways/down) on whether each belongs in KNOW or QUESTION.
framework.teacherMoves: Give pairs 3 minutes to write their two sticky notes. While they write, circulate and prompt any pair that is stuck: 'What is the one thing you are sure of from the construction today?' and 'What is one thing you still do not understand about the uji cups?' After posting, read 4–5 KNOW notes and 3–4 QUESTION notes aloud. For each KNOW note, ask the class: 'Agree? Evidence?' — WAIT 8 seconds — quick show of hands. For each QUESTION note, say: 'Good question. Is this a question we can answer today, or do we need more lessons?' Highlight with a star any question that anticipates Lesson 4 (area scale factor). Say: 'Look at this question — [read a k² question]. That is exactly where we are heading next lesson. Hold onto that thought.' Point to the uji cups on the demonstration table: 'We can now predict where the image of any point on a cup would land if we enlarged it. But we still cannot fully explain why doubling the height AND the diameter gives us four times the water. That is Lesson 4.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative Knowledge Wall (DQB Update) — the Driving Question Board makes the class's collective understanding visible and dynamic. By distinguishing KNOW from QUESTION, learners practise epistemic humility (acknowledging what is not yet explained) while celebrating genuine progress. The teacher's live vote on each sticky note creates a low-stakes peer-review of claims, reinforcing that knowledge must be evidence-backed.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher reads all KNOW notes quickly. Indicators of solid understanding: notes mention 'lengths multiply by k', 'angles stay equal', 'centre O fixed'. Indicators of confusion: notes that say 'the shape changes' or 'the image is always bigger' (forgetting k < 1 case). Teacher photographs the DQB at the end of the lesson for comparison with later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner opens their individual 'Similarity Model' — a cumulative diagram started in Lesson 1 showing the three uji cups side by side with annotated measurements. Today, learners add a new layer: they sketch a ray from a marked centre O through one key point on the small cup (e.g., the top rim), extend it to the medium cup and to the large cup, and annotate: 'O to rim (small) = d; O to rim (medium) = 2d; O to rim (large) = 3d.' They also add a two-column table to their model titled 'What Scales | What Stays the Same' and fill in at least two rows for each column. Finally, learners write a one-sentence revision to their model summary at the bottom of the page, updating their answer to the driving question: 'Doubling the size of the uji cup means every length doubles, but the area of the circle doubles TWICE because…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Similarity Model from Lesson 1. You are going to add the construction idea to it — show me that the uji cups are literally enlargements of each other from a centre point O.' Give learners 5 minutes to draw and annotate. Circulate and prompt with: 'Where would O be if the three cups are enlargements of each other? Does it matter exactly where O is, as long as the ratios are right?' — WAIT 10 seconds per learner before offering a hint. With 2 minutes remaining, say: 'Now write your one-sentence revision at the bottom. Use the words: k, lengths, angles, area.' Cold-call 2 learners to read their revision sentence aloud. After each one, ask the class: 'Does that sentence answer part of our driving question — why doubling the cup gives eight times the volume? What is still missing from the sentence?' — WAIT 12 seconds. Close the lesson by pointing to the DQB: 'Our model is growing. We can now construct any enlargement and predict lengths. Next lesson, we will prove that areas grow as k² — and that will bring us one step closer to explaining the full uji cup mystery.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision — the individual Similarity Model is a running artefact that grows across all 8 lessons. Each revision forces learners to integrate new knowledge with prior understanding rather than treating each lesson as isolated. The 'What Scales | What Stays the Same' table builds the conceptual foundation for the k² and k³ results in Lessons 4 and 5 by making the distinction between invariant (angles) and variant (lengths) properties explicit and visual.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher collects or photographs 4–5 model sheets at the end of the lesson. Success indicators: the ray diagram correctly shows O to small-cup point = d, O to medium = 2d, O to large = 3d; the two-column table correctly lists 'lengths' under 'scales' and 'angles' under 'stays the same'; the revision sentence includes k and either 'k²' or 'both dimensions scale by k'. A learner who writes 'area doubles when k = 2' has not yet internalised the k² result and needs a brief one-on-one follow-up at the start of Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Observe phase, did all learners correctly place image vertices on the ray FROM O (not on a parallel ray or a translated position)? If not, which specific step in the four-step protocol caused the error — and how will I reteach that step at the start of Lesson 4?
2. When I posed the connection question ('why did the medium uji cup need four small cups, not two?'), how many pairs reasoned to k² independently versus needing my Socratic prompting? What does this tell me about readiness for the formal area scale factor lesson?
3. Were the 'QUESTION' sticky notes on the DQB genuine mathematical questions (e.g., 'what happens to area when k = 3?') or surface-level procedural questions (e.g., 'how do I use a ruler more accurately?')? How can I nudge the class toward deeper conceptual questions next lesson?
4. Did the k = ½ reduction task (Task 3, the Kisumu cartographer context) produce any additional misconceptions — for example, learners placing the image BETWEEN O and the object versus beyond the object? How prevalent was this error?
5. Looking at the revision sentences in the Model Building phase, how many learners used the phrase 'both dimensions scale by k' or equivalent reasoning? Is the class ready to formalise the area scale factor formula in Lesson 4, or do I need a brief bridging activity at the start of that lesson?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners constructed enlargements of triangles and rectangles using three different scale factors (k = 2, k = 3, k = ½) from a centre of enlargement O, then measured every pair of corresponding sides and angles to verify their constructions. They saw that the image is always farther from O (for k > 1) or closer to O (for k < 1), and that the verification table consistently showed the length ratio equal to k and the angles equal.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Under enlargement by scale factor k: (1) every length in the image equals k times the corresponding object length; (2) every angle in the image equals the corresponding object angle — shape is preserved; (3) the centre of enlargement O remains fixed. A scale factor k > 1 enlarges; 0 < k < 1 reduces. These results hold for ANY pair of corresponding lengths — not just selected sides.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: This explains part of the uji cup phenomenon: because the cups are enlargements of each other, every single length on the medium cup is exactly k = 2 times the matching length on the small cup. The circular cross-section has both its radius AND its height scaled by k = 2. Since area involves two length dimensions multiplied together, the area scales by k × k = k² = 4 — which is exactly why four small cups of water were needed to fill the medium cup's cross-section, not two.

LESSONS.title: Area Scale Factor: Why Does the Uji Cup Label Need Nine Times as Much Paper?

slo.purpose: Learners discover and formalise the relationship between the linear scale factor k and the area scale factor k², using cut-out similar rectangles and squares, and apply this relationship to explain the anchoring phenomenon of the uji cups.
slo.knowledge: Area scale factor of similar figures = k², where k is the linear scale factor; the cross-sectional area of a circle scales by k² when the radius is multiplied by k.
slo.skills: Measure dimensions of similar cut-out figures; compute ratios of corresponding areas; tabulate results for k = 2, 3, 4; identify and generalise the k² pattern; apply the pattern to explain and predict real-world scaling situations.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the power of mathematical generalisation; develop curiosity about why nature and manufactured objects follow scale-factor rules; show responsibility by handling shared cut-out resources carefully and taking turns during group work.
slo.keyInquiry: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–3 learners identified similar figures, located centres of enlargement, and measured linear scale factors from the uji cups. They were puzzled that the medium cup needed FOUR small cups of water to fill its cross-section, not two. Lesson 4 resolves that puzzle: by measuring the areas of similar cut-out figures for k = 2, 3, 4, learners discover that area scales by k², not k. They return to the uji cups and explain the cross-sectional mystery. This k² relationship is recorded on the Driving Question Board as the second layer of the cumulative class model.
slo.safetyNotes: Scissors are used during cut-out preparation (pre-cut by teacher if time is limited). Remind learners to pass scissors handle-first, keep them flat on the desk when not in use, and not to run with scissors. No other significant hazards.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin with a prediction: if a rectangle is enlarged by a linear scale factor of k = 3, how many times larger is its area? After recording predictions, they work in groups with pre-prepared sets of similar squares and rectangles (original and images for k = 2, 3, 4) cut from manila paper. They measure dimensions, compute areas, tabulate the area ratios, and discover the pattern area scale factor = k². The teacher then returns to the anchoring phenomenon — the three uji cups — and learners use their new formula to explain why four small cups fill the cross-section of the medium cup and nine fill that of the large cup. The lesson closes with learners revising their cumulative DQB model to include the k² layer, and a brief exit task where they predict the area of a shamba (farm plot) image given the original area and the linear scale factor.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a half-sheet showing a small rectangle labelled 'Original' (4 cm × 3 cm) and is told its image has been enlarged with k = 3. Without measuring or calculating, learners individually write two predictions on a sticky note: (1) What are the dimensions of the image? (2) How many times bigger is the area of the image compared to the original? Learners stick their predictions on a class 'Prediction Wall' drawn on the chalkboard under two columns: 'Dimensions ×3' and 'Area ×?'.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the half-sheets face-down. Say: 'Before you turn the sheet over, I want you to think only about what you already know from our last three lessons. We found that linear scale factor k tells us how many times each LENGTH grows. Now here is the big question — does AREA also grow by the same factor?' Allow 10 seconds of silent thinking (WAIT TIME). Then say: 'Turn your sheet over. Write your two predictions on the sticky note. You have 3 minutes — this is individual thinking time, no discussing yet.' After 3 minutes, cold-call 5 learners (mix of confident and hesitant) to read their area predictions aloud. Record the spread of responses on the board (common answers will be ×3, ×6, ×9). Do NOT correct yet. Say: 'We have three different predictions. By the end of today's lesson, you will know with certainty which is right — and more importantly, WHY.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit-and-record prediction: surfacing prior conceptions before instruction creates cognitive dissonance that motivates the investigation. Recording the spread of predictions publicly gives every learner a personal stake in the outcome.
framework.formativeAssessment: Scan the sticky-note predictions. If more than 60% of learners predict ×3 (the most common misconception — assuming area scales linearly), note this and plan to return to it explicitly during the Explain phase. If most predict ×9, proceed but still require them to prove it empirically.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 receive an envelope containing sets of pre-cut similar figures: Set A — three squares with sides 2 cm, 4 cm, and 6 cm (k = 2 and k = 3 relative to the smallest); Set B — three rectangles with dimensions 3 cm × 2 cm, 6 cm × 4 cm, and 9 cm × 6 cm. Each group also receives a blank recording table with columns: Figure | Length (cm) | Width (cm) | Area (cm²) | Ratio of Areas (Image:Original) | k | k². Learners measure all dimensions with rulers, compute all areas, fill in the table, and compute the ratios. They then add a k = 4 row by drawing (on squared paper) a 4th rectangle scaled by k = 4 from the original 3 cm × 2 cm rectangle, measure it, and complete the row. After completing the table, each group plots 'k' on the x-axis and 'Area Ratio' on the y-axis on a provided grid and connects the points.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute envelopes and recording sheets. Say: 'Your job right now is to be measurement scientists — like surveyors mapping plots of land in the Rift Valley. Measure carefully to the nearest millimetre, calculate the areas, and fill in every cell of your table. Do not skip the k² column — compute it even if you do not yet know why it is there.' Circulate continuously. At the 8-minute mark, cold-call one group: 'Group 3, what area did you get for the 4 cm × 4 cm square?' Confirm or prompt correction. At the 14-minute mark, pause the class: 'Raise your hand if your Area Ratio for k = 2 is 4.' Count hands aloud. 'Raise your hand if your Area Ratio for k = 3 is 9.' Count hands. Say: 'Look at your k² column. What do you notice?' Allow 15 seconds WAIT TIME. Cold-call 3 groups to share their observation. For the k = 4 extension row, circulate and check that learners are drawing the rectangle accurately on squared paper (12 cm × 8 cm) before they measure.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-table pattern recognition: by computing both the area ratio AND k² side-by-side in the same table, learners are guided to notice the numerical equivalence themselves rather than being told. The graph converts the pattern into a visual curve (parabola), reinforcing that the relationship is non-linear.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check recording tables for two indicators: (1) correct area computations (e.g., 2×2=4, 4×4=16, ratio=4=2²; 3×2=6, 6×4=24, ratio=4=2²); (2) the k² column matches the area ratio column in every row. Groups with mismatched columns have either a measurement error or an arithmetic error — redirect them to re-measure before moving on. If a group's graph shows a straight line rather than a curve, this is a red flag — prompt: 'What is the area ratio when k=1? When k=2? When k=3? Can a straight line pass through all three points?'

framework.learnerExperience: The class reconvenes. Learners first revisit their sticky-note predictions on the Prediction Wall and individually mark their prediction as correct or incorrect. The teacher facilitates a whole-class discussion to formalise the rule: Area Scale Factor = k². Learners then apply the rule directly to the anchoring phenomenon: given that the medium uji cup has k = 2 relative to the small cup, they calculate the expected cross-sectional area ratio (k² = 4) and confirm it matches the observed '4 small cups to fill the cross-section.' They repeat for the large cup (k = 3, k² = 9). Finally, each learner completes three 'Apply It' problems in their exercise books: (A) A square shamba in Kericho has side 10 m; its image on a map has linear scale factor k = 5 — find the area of the image shamba. (B) A rectangular billboard in Nairobi is similar to a small poster; the billboard is k = 4 times taller — how many times more paint does the billboard need? (C) Two similar triangular road signs — the larger has k = 3 relative to the smaller; the smaller has area 150 cm² — find the area of the larger sign.
framework.teacherMoves: Open by returning to the Prediction Wall: 'Look at your sticky note. Now that you have the data, who predicted ×9 for k = 3? Who predicted ×3? Let us understand WHY ×3 is wrong.' Draw a 1×1 square on the board. Say: 'If I scale every side by k = 3, I get a 3×3 square. The area was 1. The new area is 9. The area grew by 3 × 3 = k × k = k².' Pause 10 seconds WAIT TIME. Ask: 'Why can we NOT just multiply the area by k?' Cold-call 4 learners. Guide to the explanation: 'Because area has TWO dimensions — length AND width — and BOTH scale by k, so the total scaling is k × k.' Then say: 'Now let us go back to our uji cups. The medium cup has k = 2. What does our formula predict for the cross-sectional area ratio?' WAIT 10 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners. Write on the board: k² = 2² = 4. Say: 'Does this match what we measured in Lesson 1? Yes — we needed 4 small cups!' Repeat for k = 3 (large cup). For the Apply It problems, give 8 minutes individual silent work, then cold-call one learner per problem to present their solution step-by-step at the board. Correct misconceptions immediately.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER): learners make a claim (area scales by k²), cite evidence (their data table), and reason through the mechanism (two-dimensional scaling). Connecting the formula to the phenomenon closes the explanatory loop and deepens retention.
framework.formativeAssessment: During Apply It, circulate and check exercise books. Look for: (A) correct answer 2500 m² (10×5=50m, 50²=2500 — note: this tests whether learners incorrectly apply k² to the side length rather than directly; the correct method is original area × k² = 100 × 25 = 2500 m²); (B) 16 times more paint (k²=16); (C) 150 × 9 = 1350 cm². A learner who gets 150 × 3 = 450 cm² for (C) is still applying the linear scale factor to area — intervene with a targeted re-explanation using the 1×1 square diagram.

framework.learnerExperience: The class gathers around the shared DQB (a large poster or section of the chalkboard). The DQB currently shows the driving question at the top, the uji cups phenomenon diagram, the linear scale factor definition from Lesson 2, and the centre-of-enlargement construction from Lesson 3. Each group writes one new 'We now know…' statement on a coloured card (green) and sticks it onto the DQB in the 'Area' section. They also write one remaining 'We still wonder…' question on an orange card — typically these will anticipate volume (e.g., 'If area scales by k², does volume scale by k³?'). The teacher adds a large annotated arrow on the DQB connecting the k (linear) node to the new k² (area) node, labelled 'Lesson 4: Area Scale Factor.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take 3 minutes in your groups to agree on ONE thing you now know — write it on the green card — and ONE thing you still wonder — write it on the orange card. Use mathematics, not just words.' After 3 minutes, invite each group to place their cards. Read 2–3 orange 'wonder' cards aloud. Say: 'Look at these questions about volume. We have solved the cross-section mystery today. Next lesson we will investigate whether the volume mystery — why 9 small cups fill the large uji cup — follows the same kind of rule.' Draw the arrow on the DQB explicitly and label it. End by re-reading the driving question aloud: 'Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much? We have now explained part of this — the area part. The volume part is coming.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Public knowledge-building on the DQB: making the class's growing understanding visible and cumulative reinforces metacognition — learners see their own intellectual progress — and sets up productive anticipation for the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read the green 'We now know' cards to check for accurate use of the k² formula. A card that says only 'area gets bigger' without referencing k² indicates incomplete understanding. A card that says 'area scale factor = k² because both length and width are multiplied by k' indicates strong understanding. Count the ratio of precise to vague cards as a class-level comprehension indicator.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner opens their individual Model Building Journal (an exercise book maintained across all 8 lessons). In Lessons 1–3 they drew a diagram of the three uji cups with arrows showing the linear scale factor k. Today they add a new layer: they draw two similar rectangles (the original and an image with k = 3) side-by-side, label all dimensions, and annotate: 'Area of image = k² × Area of original = 9 × Area of original.' They also add a speech bubble next to the medium uji cup: 'Cross-section area ×4 because k=2 and k²=4.' At the bottom of the page, learners write a one-sentence predictive model statement: 'I predict that if we scale all lengths of the uji cup by k, the volume will scale by ___ because ___.' (This intentionally foreshadows Lesson 5.)
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Model Building Journal to the next blank page. You have 7 minutes to draw and annotate your updated model. The model must include: your similar rectangles with dimensions labelled, the formula Area Scale Factor = k², and the updated uji cup diagram. Finally, write your prediction sentence about volume — do not leave it blank, even if you are not sure. A good scientist makes a prediction and then tests it.' Circulate and give specific verbal feedback: 'I can see you have k² labelled — can you also show me WHERE the k² comes from geometrically, by drawing the small square nine times fitting inside the large square?' With 2 minutes remaining, cold-call 2 learners to share their prediction sentences. Record the two most common volume predictions on the board (likely k² and k³) for reference at the start of Lesson 5.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision: each lesson's model entry builds on the previous, creating a personal artefact that tracks conceptual growth. The forced prediction sentence activates forward-looking reasoning and creates the cognitive hook for the next lesson's investigation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect Model Building Journals (or photograph the pages) at the end of the lesson. Check for: (1) correct labelling of dimensions and k² annotation; (2) the uji cup speech bubble correctly showing ×4 for k=2; (3) a prediction sentence that attempts to generalise to volume (any prediction is acceptable — what matters is that learners are reasoning forward). Flag journals with no prediction sentence or with a drawing that confuses the image and original for targeted follow-up at the start of Lesson 5.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) What percentage of learners correctly predicted ×k² (rather than ×k) before the investigation — and did the balance shift by the end of the Explain phase? If more than 40% still showed the ×k misconception in the Apply It problems, plan a 5-minute recap at the start of Lesson 5 using a concrete 'tile the floor' visual. (2) Did the data-table activity take longer than planned? If groups struggled with ruler measurement accuracy, consider pre-printing the cut-outs with dimensions already labelled for lower-readiness groups. (3) Which 'We still wonder' orange cards best capture genuine curiosity about volume? Use the most insightful one as the opening hook for Lesson 5. (4) Did the connection between the formula and the anchoring phenomenon feel genuine to learners, or did it feel forced? If learners did not spontaneously connect k²=4 to '4 small cups,' plan a more explicit physical demonstration at the start of Lesson 5 (e.g., actually pouring water into circular cross-sections cut from card). (5) Were all learners able to access the Apply It problems, or did some learners need scaffolding on basic area computation before they could engage with the scale factor concept? Identify these learners for peer-support pairing in Lesson 5.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners measured and compared the areas of sets of similar squares and rectangles (with k = 2, 3, 4) cut from manila paper, recorded their data in a structured table, and plotted area ratio against k on a graph.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The area scale factor of similar figures equals k² (the square of the linear scale factor), because both length and width are each multiplied by k, making the total area grow by k × k. This explains why the cross-sectional area of the medium uji cup (k = 2) is 4 times — not 2 times — the cross-section of the small cup.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Using the k² rule, learners explained and predicted how the cross-sectional area of a similar shape changes when the linear scale factor is known, and applied this to real-world contexts including shamba areas in Kericho, billboard paint coverage in Nairobi, and triangular road signs.

LESSONS.title: Volume Scale Factor: Why the Large Uji Cup Holds Eight Times as Much

slo.purpose: By the end of this lesson, learners will be able to determine the volume scale factor of similar solids and explain why scaling all linear dimensions of a container by k multiplies its volume by k³.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (i) volume scale factor = k³ where k is the linear scale factor; (ii) this relationship holds for all similar solids (cubes, cuboids, cylinders, sufuria, uji cups); (iii) the three scale factors relate as: linear k → area k² → volume k³.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (i) measure the dimensions of similar solids and compute their volumes; (ii) tabulate and calculate the ratio of volumes for k = 2 and k = 3; (iii) use volume scale factor to predict the volume of any similar solid without re-measuring; (iv) explain the anchoring phenomenon fully using the k³ rule.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that mathematical patterns discovered through hands-on measurement are powerful predictive tools, and will develop confidence in using those patterns to solve real-life design and packaging problems encountered in Kenyan contexts such as catering, pottery, and container manufacturing.
slo.keyInquiry: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 3–4 learners established that area scales by k². Now in Lesson 5 they extend that reasoning one dimension further: they physically measure and compute the volumes of similar Kasuku tins and model cubes/cuboids, discover the k³ pattern, and for the first time can fully explain the anchoring phenomenon — why the large uji cup needs nine small cups of water (k = 3, so volume scale factor = 3³ = 27 ÷ 3 = 9 cross-section portions, and fully 27 times the volume). The DQB is updated with k³ and the complete chain k → k² → k³ is now visible.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners handle water and tins — wipe spills immediately to prevent slipping. No sharp cutting tools are used in this lesson. Learners should handle Kasuku tins carefully to avoid sharp edges on cut lids.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by revisiting the uji cup phenomenon and predicting how many small cups will fill the large cup when k = 3. They then measure the dimensions of two sets of similar solids (model cubes/cuboids OR small and large Kasuku tins) and compute volumes, tabulating the volume ratio for k = 2 and k = 3. Through structured discussion (Think-Pair-Share and data pooling on the board), they discover that volume scale factor = k³. They apply this rule to explain the anchoring phenomenon fully and connect it to the sufuria supporting phenomenon. The DQB is updated to record the complete scale-factor chain. A model-building activity asks learners to revise their cumulative diagrams to include the k³ relationship. Formative assessment is embedded throughout via whiteboards, cold-calling, and a 3-question exit ticket.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown the three uji cups from the anchoring phenomenon (or a diagram/photograph of them on the board). They are reminded that in Lesson 4 they proved the label (surface area) of the large cup (k = 3) needs 9 times as much paper as the small cup. The teacher now poses: 'We have never directly measured how many small cups of water fill the large cup. Based on everything you now know about k and k², what is YOUR prediction for the volume ratio when k = 3? Write your prediction AND your reasoning on your mini-whiteboard. Do not discuss yet.' Learners write individual predictions (expected range: some say 3×, some say 9×, some who are beginning to generalise say 27×). After 2 minutes of silent writing, the teacher calls on 5 learners cold-call (by name from the register, not volunteers) to share predictions and reasoning. The teacher records all unique predictions on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions — Volume Ratio for k = 3' without affirming or correcting any.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Display the uji cup diagram/photograph prominently. Say: 'Look at the small cup and the large cup. Every length on the large cup is exactly 3 times the corresponding length on the small cup — that is our k = 3.' WAIT 5 seconds. 'In Lesson 4 we proved the surface area ratio is 9 — that is k² = 3² = 9. Today we go one step further: VOLUME. How many small cups of water do you think will fill the large cup?' 2. Say: 'Write your numerical prediction AND at least one sentence of reasoning on your whiteboard. You have 2 minutes. Work silently.' Start timer visibly. 3. After 2 minutes, cold-call exactly 5 learners: 'Amina — share your prediction and reasoning.' WAIT 10 seconds after each learner speaks before responding or moving on. 4. Record all predictions on the board without evaluation: e.g. '3×', '6×', '9×', '27×'. Say: 'We have several different predictions. Today's experiment will tell us who is right — and more importantly, WHY.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Individual Prediction with Public Commitment: By writing predictions before any instruction and having them recorded publicly, learners create cognitive stakes in the outcome. This activates prior knowledge from Lessons 3–4 (k and k²) and primes them to look for the pattern that resolves the discrepancy between predictions.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: All learners have a numerical prediction on their whiteboard within 2 minutes. Teacher scans boards while circulating — note any learners who write '27' with correct reasoning (k³ anticipated) and any who write '3' (still holding linear intuition). This informs pacing: if more than half predict 27 correctly with reasoning, compress Phase 2 to 15 minutes and extend Phase 3 discussion.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4. Each group receives: (a) a set of 3 similar wooden or cardboard model cubes with side lengths approximately 2 cm, 4 cm, and 6 cm (k = 1, 2, 3 relative to the smallest), OR (b) a small Kasuku tin and a large Kasuku tin whose diameter and height are in ratio 1:2. Groups also receive a 30 cm ruler, a recording worksheet, and a calculator. PART A — Measurement and Computation (15 min): Learners measure the length, width, and height (or radius and height for cylinders) of each solid to the nearest millimetre and record in the worksheet table. They then compute the volume of each solid using the appropriate formula (V = l × w × h for cuboids; V = πr²h for cylinders). They calculate the ratio Volume₂ / Volume₁ (large ÷ small) for k = 2 and Volume₃ / Volume₁ (largest ÷ small) for k = 3, and record these ratios as decimals and as fractions. PART B — Class Data Pool (8 min): One representative from each group writes their group's results on the shared class table on the board (pre-drawn with columns: Group | k | Measured volume ratio | k² | k³). All groups' data is now visible. PART C — Pattern Identification (5 min): Learners examine the class table and write ONE sentence on their whiteboard answering: 'What do you notice about the volume ratio column and the k³ column?'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Distribute materials. Say: 'Your task has two parts. Part A: measure, compute volumes, and find the ratio. Part B: add your results to the class table. You have 15 minutes for Part A.' Display the worksheet structure on the board. 2. Circulate actively. Stop at each group for at least 60 seconds. Use targeted prompts: 'How did you decide which formula to use?' WAIT 10 seconds. 'What units will your volume be in?' WAIT 10 seconds. 'Before you divide — what do you expect the ratio to be based on our predictions?' 3. After 15 min, say: 'One spokesperson per group — write your k, your measured volume ratio, k², and k³ in the class table. You have 3 minutes.' 4. Once the table is filled, give learners 2 minutes to examine it silently. Then say: 'Write ONE sentence on your whiteboard: what pattern do you see between the volume ratio column and the k³ column?' WAIT 15 seconds of full silence. 5. Cold-call 4 learners (choose at least one from a group that used cylinders and one from a group that used cuboids): 'Kamau, read your sentence.' WAIT 10 seconds after each. 6. Affirm the pattern: 'Every group found that the volume ratio equals k³ — even though some of you used cubes, some used cuboids, and some used Kasuku tins. The shape does not matter. The rule is: volume scale factor = k³.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Pooling + Cross-Group Comparison: By pooling data from groups using different solid shapes (cubes, cuboids, cylinders), learners see that the k³ rule is shape-independent. This is a deliberate generalisation move — the pattern is more convincing when it appears across different physical objects than when seen in a single case.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each group's worksheet table is complete with correct volume calculations (teacher checks units — cm³ — and formula use during circulation). (2) Volume ratios in the class table are approximately 8 (for k = 2) and 27 (for k = 3) — flag any group with a ratio far from these for immediate re-measurement support. (3) Whiteboard sentences explicitly mention 'k³' or 'cube of k' — learners who write only 'it is bigger' need a targeted question: 'By exactly how much? Compare the ratio number to k and to k².'

framework.learnerExperience: PART A — Conceptual Explanation (8 min): The teacher leads a whole-class structured explanation of WHY volume scales by k³, using a visual decomposition on the board. For a cube of side 1 unit: V = 1³ = 1. Scale by k = 2: each side becomes 2, V = 2³ = 8. The teacher shows that you can fit exactly 8 copies of the small cube inside the large cube by drawing a 2×2×2 grid inside the larger cube. Learners copy the diagram into their notebooks and annotate it for k = 3 (showing a 3×3×3 = 27 grid). PART B — Phenomenon Explanation (7 min): Learners work individually for 4 minutes to write a full explanation (3–5 sentences) answering: 'Using the k³ rule, explain exactly why the large uji cup (k = 3) needs 27 small cups of water to fill it completely — not 3 and not 9.' They then share with a partner (Think-Pair-Share, 3 minutes). PART C — Sufuria Connection (5 min): The teacher poses: 'Mama Wanjiku has a small sufuria and a large sufuria. The large sufuria has a diameter twice as big as the small one AND is twice as tall. She wants to cook ugali for a wedding. How many times more maize flour does she need compared to using the small sufuria?' Learners solve individually on whiteboards (answer: k = 2, volume scale factor = 2³ = 8 — she needs 8 times as much flour). Cold-call 3 learners to share and justify.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Draw a 1×1×1 cube on the board. Say: 'Volume = 1³ = 1 cubic unit. Now I scale every side by k = 2.' Draw the 2×2×2 cube beside it. 'Volume = 2³ = 8. But WHY 8? Watch.' Draw grid lines inside the large cube showing 2 layers, 2 rows, 2 columns. 'I can fit exactly 8 small cubes inside. One dimension gives me k = 2 copies. Two dimensions give me k² = 4. Three dimensions give me k³ = 8.' 2. Say: 'Now YOU draw this for k = 3 in your notebook — show the 3×3×3 grid. You have 3 minutes.' WAIT. Cold-call one learner to the board to draw their version. 3. Say: 'Now connect this to our uji cups. Write 3–5 sentences explaining why the large uji cup needs 27 small cups — not 3, not 9. Use the words: linear scale factor, volume scale factor, k³. You have 4 minutes.' WAIT. 4. Pair-share: 'Share with your partner. One of you reads, the other checks: did they mention k = 3, k³ = 27, and connect it to the three dimensions of the cup?' 3 minutes. 5. Cold-call 2 pairs to share their explanation. After each, ask the class: 'Thumbs up if their explanation mentioned all three: k, k³, and the three dimensions of the cup.' 6. Sufuria problem: Read aloud slowly. Say: 'On your whiteboard — what is k? What is the volume scale factor? How many times more flour?' WAIT 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners. Confirm: 'k = 2, volume scale factor = 2³ = 8. Mama Wanjiku needs 8 times more flour. This is exactly the same mathematics as our uji cup — just a different container.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Visual Decomposition + Phenomenon Re-Explanation: The 3D grid diagram makes the abstract k³ formula concrete and countable. Requiring learners to write the phenomenon explanation in their own words (then stress-test it with a partner) ensures they are not just reciting a formula but can deploy it as an explanatory tool. The sufuria transfer problem checks whether they can apply k³ to a new Kenyan context.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Notebooks show a correctly drawn 3×3×3 grid with 27 small cubes visible (teacher circulates and stamps or ticks correct diagrams). (2) Written phenomenon explanations include the words 'k = 3', 'k³ = 27', and reference to three spatial dimensions — flag any explanation that says '9 × 3 = 27' without explaining WHY multiplication occurs in a third dimension. (3) Sufuria whiteboard answers show 'k = 2, 2³ = 8' — any learner who writes '2² = 4' is still conflating area and volume scale factors and needs targeted re-teaching in Phase 4 or as homework.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher directs learners' attention to the class DQB (a large chart or section of the board that has been accumulating across all 8 lessons). Learners review what is already posted: Lesson 1 — phenomenon observations and initial questions; Lesson 2 — properties of similar figures and linear scale factor k; Lesson 3 — linear scale factor k confirmed with measurements; Lesson 4 — area scale factor k². Now the class adds the new understanding from Lesson 5. Each learner writes on a sticky note (or a strip of paper): one CLAIM (something they now know for certain) and one QUESTION (something they are still wondering about or want to explore). Claims are posted under the green 'We Now Know' column; questions under the yellow 'We Are Still Wondering' column. The teacher then draws attention to the complete scale-factor chain now visible on the DQB: k → k² → k³, and asks learners to suggest what real-life design questions this chain might help answer (expected: 'How do engineers design containers of different sizes?', 'How do architects scale up buildings?', 'Why does a large sufuria cost so much more to make than a small one?').
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Point to the DQB. Say: 'Let's look at where we started and how far we have come.' Read aloud the original phenomenon question posted in Lesson 1. 2. Walk through each lesson's addition briefly: 'Lesson 2 — we found k. Lesson 3 — we confirmed k with measurements. Lesson 4 — we discovered k². Today — we discovered k³.' As you name each, point to the relevant sticky notes or entries. 3. Distribute sticky notes. Say: 'Write ONE claim — something you are now certain is true — and ONE question you still have. You have 3 minutes. Write in full sentences.' WAIT. 4. Invite 4 learners (cold-call) to read their claim aloud before posting it. After each, ask: 'Class — do we agree this is a proven claim? Thumbs up or thumbs sideways.' 5. Post all notes. Then draw a large arrow on the board connecting k → k² → k³. Say: 'This chain is the mathematical heart of our unit. In Lessons 6 and 7 we will use it to solve real design problems. In Lesson 8 we will bring it all back to our uji cups one final time.' 6. Read 2–3 of the 'still wondering' questions aloud. Say: 'These are excellent mathematical questions. Keep them in mind as we continue.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Claim-and-Question Protocol: Distinguishing 'what we know' from 'what we are still wondering' develops metacognitive awareness of the boundary between evidence and inference. Publicly posting the k → k² → k³ chain gives learners a visual organiser of the unit's conceptual arc and positions them to anticipate future lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Claims are specific and evidence-based (e.g. 'Volume scale factor = k³, proven by our Kasuku tin measurements') rather than vague (e.g. 'big things are bigger'). (2) Questions are mathematically productive (e.g. 'Does k³ work for spheres too?') rather than procedural (e.g. 'How do you calculate volume?'). Teacher photographs the DQB at the end of this phase for record-keeping and to share on the ARES platform.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their cumulative model diagram begun in Lesson 2 and revised in Lessons 3 and 4 (a labelled drawing or concept map showing a small solid and a large similar solid with annotations). They now add the volume scale factor layer: they draw a third annotation arrow on their diagram labelled 'Volume scale factor = k³' and add a worked numerical example for k = 3 (showing 3³ = 27). They also add a brief 'phenomenon connection' box: 'Large uji cup (k = 3): volume = 27 × small cup. Needs 27 small cups of water.' Learners who finish early extend their model to include the complete chain k → k² → k³ in a table format with columns for k = 1, 2, 3, 4. The lesson closes with a 3-question exit ticket on mini-whiteboards: Q1 — 'A small cube has side 3 cm. A similar cube has side 9 cm. What is k?' (Answer: 3). Q2 — 'What is the volume scale factor?' (Answer: 27). Q3 — 'If the small cube holds 27 cm³ of water, how much does the large cube hold?' (Answer: 729 cm³). Learners hold up whiteboards simultaneously on the teacher's signal.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Say: 'Take out your cumulative model diagram. You are going to add today's discovery.' Display the previous lesson's model structure on the board as a reference. 2. Say: 'Add a third arrow for volume scale factor = k³. Add a worked example for k = 3. Add a phenomenon connection box. You have 6 minutes.' WAIT. Circulate. Prompt any learner who has not yet connected the model to the uji cups: 'Where on your diagram can you show that the large uji cup holds 27 times as much as the small cup?' 3. After 6 minutes say: 'Pause your diagrams. Exit ticket — three quick questions on your whiteboards.' Read Q1 aloud. 'Write only your answer — you have 20 seconds.' WAIT 20 seconds. 'Boards up.' Scan all boards. Affirm or correct briefly. Repeat for Q2 and Q3. 4. Close: 'Today we completed the scale-factor chain: k for lengths, k² for areas, k³ for volumes. We can now fully explain our uji cup mystery. In Lesson 6 we will use all three scale factors to solve real design problems — including designing containers for a Nairobi catering company. Well done.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: Requiring learners to physically add to a diagram they have been building across five lessons externalises the growth of their understanding. The layered model (k, then k², then k³) makes the mathematical structure visible as a coherent system, not three isolated facts. The simultaneous whiteboard exit ticket gives the teacher a rapid whole-class snapshot of mastery before the lesson ends.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Cumulative models show three correctly labelled annotation arrows (k, k², k³) with numerical examples — models missing any layer indicate incomplete integration of prior lessons. (2) Exit ticket Q1: all boards show '3' — any board showing '6' or '1/3' indicates confusion about direction of scale factor. (3) Q2: boards show '27' — any board showing '9' indicates conflation of area and volume scale factors (priority re-teaching target). (4) Q3: boards show '729' — any board showing '243' (multiplied by 9 not 27) confirms the k² vs k³ confusion. Teacher records names of learners with incorrect Q2 or Q3 for follow-up in Lesson 6 opener.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) Did the class data pool in Phase 2 show consistent k³ ratios across all groups, or did measurement errors obscure the pattern for some groups? If ratios were inconsistent, consider whether the model cubes/Kasuku tins were sufficiently precise — pre-measuring and marking the solids before the lesson may help in future iterations. (2) In Phase 3, how many learners were still conflating area and volume scale factors (writing 9 instead of 27 on the sufuria problem)? If more than 25% of learners made this error, begin Lesson 6 with a 5-minute retrieval activity comparing k, k², and k³ side by side before moving to applications. (3) Were the DQB 'still wondering' questions mathematically productive? If learners are not yet asking questions about new shapes (spheres, cones) or real-life design, the phenomenon connection may not yet be deep enough — consider assigning a home observation task: 'Find two similar containers at home and measure their dimensions. What do you predict the volume ratio will be?' (4) Were all five phases completed within 80 minutes? The most common time pressure is Phase 2 (measurement) — if groups are slow, pre-fill one row of the class table as a model before the lesson begins. (5) Note the names of learners flagged in exit ticket Q2 and Q3 and ensure they are seated near a strong peer explainer in Lesson 6 group work.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners measured the dimensions of similar solids (model cubes/cuboids or Kasuku tins with k = 2 and k = 3) and computed their volumes. They pooled class data in a shared table showing the measured volume ratio alongside k², and k³ for each scale factor.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The volume scale factor of similar solids equals k³, where k is the linear scale factor. This means that when every length is scaled by k = 3, the volume becomes 3³ = 27 times as large. The complete chain is now established: length scales by k, area by k², and volume by k³.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained the anchoring phenomenon fully: the large uji cup (k = 3) needs 27 small cups of water — not 3 and not 9 — because volume is a three-dimensional quantity and each of the three dimensions is multiplied by k, giving k × k × k = k³. They also applied this to the sufuria supporting phenomenon, confirming that a sufuria with k = 2 holds 2³ = 8 times as much ugali porridge as the small sufuria.
