LESSONS.title: Relating Linear, Area and Volume Scale Factors — The Unified k, k², k³ Model

slo.purpose: Learners consolidate the three scaling relationships (k, k², k³) into a single unified mathematical model, solve mixed real-life problems involving similar solids, and build a complete annotated diagram-and-formula summary that advances the class Driving Question Board.
slo.knowledge: Learners know that for two similar figures or solids with linear scale factor k: corresponding lengths scale by k, corresponding surface areas scale by k², and corresponding volumes scale by k³. They can state and apply all three relationships simultaneously from a single given value of k.
slo.skills: Learners can: (a) construct and interpret a unified k / k² / k³ table for any given linear scale factor; (b) solve mixed problems requiring calculation of paint needed (area) and water held (volume) for similar tanks; (c) use digital devices to verify scale-factor calculations; (d) produce a fully annotated model (diagram + formula summary) in their notebooks and on the class DQB.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the power and elegance of a single number k encoding three different scaling behaviours, and develop confidence in applying this unified model to predict real-world quantities such as paint, water capacity, and material costs for structures across Kenya.
slo.keyInquiry: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lessons 1–5 established the phenomenon (the Shrinking Uji Cup), identified properties of similar figures, introduced the linear scale factor, and explored area and volume scale factors separately. Lesson 6 is the pivotal consolidation lesson: learners tie all three relationships together into one coherent model. Using the Rift Valley water-tank context, they solve problems that require choosing the correct scale factor (k, k², or k³) for a given physical quantity, verify answers with digital devices, and update both their notebook models and the class DQB with the complete formula summary — directly answering the driving question for the first time with full mathematical precision.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials are used. If learners bring physical containers for demonstration, ensure surfaces are dry to prevent slipping. Supervise responsible use of digital devices and enforce the school's online-safety guidelines when accessing the Kenya Education Cloud or any online simulation.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 6 (80 min) is the consolidation and model-building apex of the Similarity and Enlargement sequence. The teacher opens by projecting an image of two real water tanks from the Rift Valley (or a hand-drawn diagram) and poses a mixed-context challenge: given a linear scale factor of 3, how many times more paint does the larger tank need, and how many times more water does it hold? Learners first predict using prior knowledge, then gather evidence by constructing a unified k / k² / k³ table and solving a structured set of mixed problems — some giving k and asking for area or volume ratios, others working backwards from area or volume ratios to find k. Digital devices are used to verify all calculations and to explore an interactive simulation on the Kenya Education Cloud. A whole-class sensemaking discussion makes the unified model explicit. Learners then build a complete annotated model (labelled diagram of the uji cups + formula box) in their notebooks, and two volunteers update the class DQB with the finished formula summary. The lesson closes with an exit-ticket problem that requires learners to apply all three relationships simultaneously.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners examine a projected image of two similar cylindrical water tanks labelled 'Nakuru Small Tank' and 'Nakuru Large Tank'. The teacher reveals that every linear dimension of the large tank is exactly 3 times that of the small tank (k = 3). Without any calculation, learners individually write three predictions in their notebooks: (i) How many times more metal sheet (surface area) is needed to build the large tank? (ii) How many times more water does the large tank hold? (iii) If it costs Ksh 4,500 to paint the small tank, how much will it cost to paint the large tank? Learners share predictions with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes, then selected pairs report to the class. The teacher records all predictions (not corrected yet) on the whiteboard under the heading 'Our Predictions — Lesson 6'.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the Rift Valley tank image and say: 'Before we calculate anything, I want your honest mathematical instincts. Write your three predictions — you have 3 minutes of silent thinking time.' [WAIT 3 minutes — do not prompt.] After pair-share, cold-call 4 pairs (select one high-confidence, one low-confidence, one who predicted k² correctly, one who predicted k³ correctly) and record all responses verbatim. Say: 'Notice we have different answers on the board. By the end of today's lesson, every one of you will be able to prove which prediction is correct — and explain exactly why.' Circle the predictions but do not reveal answers. Explicitly connect to the phenomenon: 'Remember our uji cups — we were surprised that doubling the height gave us four times the water in cross-section. Today we are going to build the complete mathematical story for that surprise.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit-and-Record Prediction Wall — recording unresolved predictions publicly creates cognitive dissonance that motivates the evidence-gathering phase and gives learners a concrete benchmark to revise against during model-building.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each learner has written three distinct numerical predictions in their notebook before pair-share begins. Teacher scans notebooks during circulation to check that predictions are numerical (not just 'more' or 'less'). Note which learners predict k² for area and k³ for volume (showing carry-forward understanding from Lessons 4–5) versus those who predict k for all three (showing the misconception to target in the Explain phase).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 4 to complete a structured Unified Scale-Factor Table activity. Each group receives (or draws in their notebook) a table with columns: [Linear Scale Factor k | Area Scale Factor | Volume Scale Factor | Example: length of edge | Example: surface area | Example: volume]. Groups complete the table for k = 2, 3, 4, and 5, using their knowledge from Lessons 4 and 5. They then open a verified digital simulation on the Kenya Education Cloud (or teacher-provided GeoGebra file) on their learner digital devices and manipulate a 3-D cylinder — increasing its radius and height by factors of 2, 3, 4, and 5 — reading off the surface area and volume displayed by the app. They record the app's computed values alongside their table entries and check for agreement. Groups that finish early attempt the extension: k = 1.5 (representing a mug that is 1.5 times the height of the toddler uji cup).
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute or project the blank Unified Scale-Factor Table template. Say: 'You have 12 minutes to complete columns 2 and 3 using what you already know from Lessons 4 and 5, then verify every entry using your digital device. If your table value and the app value disagree, that is important data — write down both and flag it for our discussion.' [Set a visible 12-minute timer.] Circulate and use targeted prompts: for groups stalling on k = 4, ask 'What is 4 squared? What is 4 cubed? How does that connect to your table?' [WAIT 10 seconds for response before elaborating.] After 12 minutes, pause the class: 'Hands up — which groups found a disagreement between their table and the app?' Address any disagreements publicly. Cold-call 3 groups to read out their k = 3 row. Say: 'Look at the row for k = 3 on your table. Freeze that row in your mind — it is the key row for our tank problem.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data-Table + Digital Verification — completing the table by hand first activates prior knowledge and forces explicit calculation, while the app verification provides immediate corrective feedback and reinforces the pattern through a second representational mode (dynamic 3-D model), deepening understanding of the k / k² / k³ relationships.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every group's table has correct entries for at least k = 2 and k = 3 (area scale factors 4 and 9; volume scale factors 8 and 27) before the Explain phase begins. Teacher checks by asking each group to hold up their table and scanning for the k = 3 row. Groups with incorrect entries are flagged for targeted support during the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher leads a whole-class worked-example sequence using the Rift Valley tank scenario as the anchor. Three connected problems are solved together on the board, with learners solving each step in their notebooks before the teacher reveals the answer: Problem A (forward, area): 'Two similar water tanks in the Rift Valley have a linear scale factor of 3. A painter charges Ksh 500 per square metre. If the small tank has a surface area of 18 m², how much will it cost to paint the large tank?' Problem B (forward, volume): 'The small tank holds 2,000 litres of water. How many litres does the large tank hold?' Problem C (inverse): 'A third tank has a surface area 25 times that of the small tank. What is the linear scale factor between the small tank and this third tank? How many times more water does it hold?' After each problem, learners compare their notebook answer with the board solution and mark it. The teacher then formally states the Unified Model: 'If two similar figures have linear scale factor k, then area scale factor = k² and volume scale factor = k³. One number — k — tells you everything.' Learners copy the boxed formula summary into their notebooks. A brief pair discussion follows: 'Looking back at our uji cups from Lesson 1 — the toddler cup was scaled by k = 2 to make the adult mug, and by k = 3 to make the catering flask. Use our unified model to explain every surprising number we measured in Lesson 1.'
framework.teacherMoves: Write Problem A on the board and say: 'Work this out individually and silently — 3 minutes.' [WAIT 3 minutes.] Then say: 'Tell me: what scale factor do we use for surface area — is it k, k², or k³? Show me with your fingers: one finger for k, two fingers for k², three fingers for k³.' [WAIT 10 seconds for whole-class finger-vote.] Cold-call 2 learners who show different answers to explain their reasoning before revealing the solution. Repeat the finger-vote protocol for Problems B and C. For Problem C, use the prompt: 'We are working backwards — we know the area ratio is 25. What operation reverses squaring?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call a learner who has written √25 = 5 in their notebook. After the formula box is copied, say: 'Turn to your partner. Use this model to explain why filling the adult uji mug needed four small cups of water, not two. You have 2 minutes.' Cold-call 2 pairs. Affirm and connect: 'You have just explained the phenomenon that puzzled us in Lesson 1. k = 2, k² = 4 — four small cups. The mathematics predicted it perfectly.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Worked-Example with Finger-Vote Checkpoints — the finger-vote forces every learner to commit to a choice (k, k², or k³) before the answer is revealed, making the decision-point cognitively explicit. Connecting back to the uji-cup phenomenon at the end of the phase reinforces that the abstract formula is the explanation for the concrete mystery learners observed in Lesson 1.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) During each finger-vote, teacher notes the ratio of correct to incorrect responses and adjusts pacing accordingly — if fewer than 70% of learners show the correct finger for Problem A, re-teach the area scale factor before proceeding to Problem B. (2) All learners have the formula box (k → lengths, k² → areas, k³ → volumes) correctly copied in their notebooks before the DQB phase begins. Teacher spot-checks 6 notebooks (2 high, 2 mid, 2 low attainment) during the pair discussion.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write one 'I now understand…' statement and one 'I still wonder…' question on separate sticky notes (or on torn notebook paper if sticky notes are unavailable). Two volunteers come to the front and update the class DQB: they add a new card titled 'The Unified Model' containing the formula summary (k → lengths, k² → areas, k³ → volumes) and attach it to the central driving question card. They also move any previously posted 'mystery' questions (e.g., 'Why did we need 9 small cups to fill the flask?' from Lesson 1) into a new column labelled 'Explained by the Unified Model'. The class briefly reviews the DQB together — identifying which sub-questions of the driving question are now answered and which remain open (e.g., applying the model to non-cylindrical shapes, and to the cost of manufacturing similar containers).
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes (or instruct learners to tear a page corner) and say: 'Write one thing you now understand about scaling — be specific, use numbers. And write one thing you are still wondering. You have 2 minutes.' [WAIT 2 minutes.] Invite volunteers for the DQB update — give them 2 minutes to arrange the cards while the class reads the board silently. Then facilitate a 3-minute whole-class scan of the DQB: 'Look at the board. Count how many of our original mystery questions from Lesson 1 can now be answered using the unified model.' Cold-call 3 learners to read one explained question and state the explanation in one sentence. Say: 'Our driving question asks why doubling a container makes it hold eight times as much. Can anyone answer that now in one sentence?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call 2 learners. Acknowledge that the remaining open questions — particularly about designing and building containers — will be the focus of Lesson 7.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Reorganisation with 'Explained' Column — physically moving mystery cards from 'open' to 'explained' gives learners a visible, tangible record of their growing understanding and makes the cumulative progress of the evidence-gathering sequence concrete. The remaining open questions sustain inquiry momentum into Lesson 7.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has produced a specific, numerical 'I now understand…' statement (e.g., 'I now understand that k = 3 means the large tank needs 9 times more paint and holds 27 times more water') rather than a vague one. Teacher reads 8–10 sticky notes during the next phase to identify persistent misconceptions for the Lesson 7 opening hook.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually construct a Complete Annotated Model in their notebooks. The model has two components: (A) a labelled diagram showing the three uji cups (toddler, adult, catering flask) with annotated scale factors — all linear dimensions labelled with ×k and ×3, all surface-area labels showing ×k² and ×9, and all volume/capacity labels showing ×k³ and ×27; (B) a Formula Summary Box containing: 'For two similar figures/solids with linear scale factor k: Length ratio = k, Area ratio = k², Volume ratio = k³' — with the Rift Valley tank numbers (k = 3: area ×9, volume ×27) given as a worked example beneath the box. Learners who finish early add a second example: the uji cups with k = 2 (adult vs toddler) and k = 3 (flask vs toddler). The lesson closes with a 5-minute individual Exit Ticket: 'Two similar matumbo (cooking pots) used at a Nairobi nyama choma restaurant are similar in shape. The large pot has a height 4 times that of the small pot. (a) How many times more metal was needed to make the large pot? (b) If the small pot holds 5 litres of soup, how much does the large pot hold? (c) If the small pot cost Ksh 800 to manufacture, estimate the manufacturing cost of the large pot, assuming cost is proportional to the metal used.' Learners submit or show the Exit Ticket to the teacher at the door.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You now have 12 minutes to build your complete annotated model — diagram plus formula box. This is your personal mathematical tool for everything that follows in this unit and in life. Make it clear enough that you could explain it to a younger sibling.' [Play soft background music or set a silent working timer for 12 minutes.] Circulate and give specific praise: 'I can see you have labelled the volume arrow ×k³ — excellent. Now add the actual numbers for k = 3 below it.' For learners who have drawn the diagram but not the formula box, prompt: 'Your diagram is strong. Now add the formula box — what are the three rules?' [WAIT 10 seconds before assisting.] At the 12-minute mark, say: 'Close your models. Here is your exit ticket — 5 minutes, individual work, no discussion.' [Distribute or display the nyama choma pot problem.] Collect tickets at the door. As learners leave, tell each one: 'In Lesson 7 we will use this model to design and build — you are ready.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Annotated Diagram + Formula Box — combining a visual representation (the labelled uji-cup diagram) with a symbolic one (the formula box) exploits dual-coding to strengthen long-term retention. Using the anchoring phenomenon as the subject of the diagram ensures that the model remains connected to the original observable mystery rather than becoming an abstract set of rules.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Exit Ticket answers: (a) k = 4, area scale factor = 16, so 16 times more metal; (b) volume scale factor = 64, so 64 × 5 = 320 litres; (c) cost proportional to area → 16 × Ksh 800 = Ksh 12,800. Teacher sorts exit tickets into three piles (all correct, partially correct, incorrect) before Lesson 7 and uses the results to plan targeted warm-up support. (2) All learner notebooks contain a complete annotated model with both diagram and formula box — checked during model-building circulation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) During the finger-vote checkpoints in the Explain phase, what percentage of learners correctly identified k² for area and k³ for volume on the first attempt — and which of the three problems (A, B, or C) produced the most incorrect responses? What does this tell you about which relationship (area vs volume vs inverse) needs reinforcement in Lesson 7? (2) Review the exit-ticket piles: did learners who correctly solved Part (a) (area scale factor) also correctly solve Part (b) (volume scale factor), or did a subset succeed on area but fail on volume? This pattern would indicate that k³ remains the weaker of the three relationships and should anchor the Lesson 7 opening. (3) Read the 'I still wonder…' sticky notes from the DQB phase: do any questions signal confusion about when to use k versus k² versus k³ (i.e., confusion about which physical quantity determines which scale factor)? If so, design a 5-minute sorting warm-up for Lesson 7 where learners categorise quantities (length of pipe, litres of paint, area of label, number of bricks) under k, k², or k³ before the new content begins. (4) Were all learners able to connect the exit-ticket pot problem back to the uji-cup phenomenon, or did some treat it as an isolated calculation? If the latter, open Lesson 7 by explicitly asking learners to narrate the connection aloud.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Two similar cylindrical water tanks from the Rift Valley with linear scale factor k = 3; a unified k / k² / k³ table completed and verified using digital devices; the GeoGebra/Kenya Education Cloud simulation showing surface area and volume changing as cylinder dimensions are scaled by k = 2, 3, 4, and 5.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: For any two similar figures or solids with linear scale factor k: corresponding lengths scale by k, corresponding surface areas scale by k², and corresponding volumes scale by k³. For k = 3: the large Rift Valley tank needs 9 times more paint (k² = 9) and holds 27 times more water (k³ = 27). This single rule — one value of k encoding three scaling behaviours — explains every surprising number observed in the Shrinking Uji Cup phenomenon since Lesson 1.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The anchoring phenomenon is now fully explained: when the uji cup manufacturer doubled every dimension (k = 2), the surface area of the label increased by k² = 4 (four times more paper) and the volume increased by k³ = 8 (eight small cups needed to fill it, not two). When dimensions were tripled (k = 3), the label needed k² = 9 times more paper and the volume needed k³ = 27 times more water (nine small cups, not three). The driving question — 'Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much?' — is answered: because volume scales as the cube of the linear scale factor, so k = 2 gives k³ = 8.

LESSONS.title: Real-Life Applications and Problem Solving — Apply & Communicate

slo.purpose: Learners apply their accumulated understanding of linear, area, and volume scale factors to multi-step, real-life problem contexts — scale drawings, recipe scaling, and map reading — and publicly communicate a full, evidence-backed answer to the driving question.
slo.knowledge: Learners know that: (i) linear scale factor k scales lengths, (ii) area scale factor k² scales surface areas, and (iii) volume scale factor k³ scales volumes; and that these relationships hold for ANY pair of similar figures or solids.
slo.skills: Learners can: (a) read and construct a scale drawing of a school building, (b) use volume scale factor to resize a recipe (e.g., a mandazi recipe scaled for a larger tin), (c) calculate real distances from a map using a stated scale, and (d) present one self-researched real-life example of similarity and enlargement to the class with supporting evidence.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the coherence and utility of similarity and enlargement across diverse real-life domains (architecture, catering, cartography) and demonstrate confidence in communicating mathematical reasoning to peers.
slo.keyInquiry: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–6, learners built the full mathematical model: they measured the uji cups, discovered the k / k² / k³ surprise, derived the scale-factor rules, and applied them to solids. Lesson 7 is the 'Apply & Communicate' capstone: learners carry those rules out of the classroom and into scale drawings of school buildings, a Kenyan catering recipe, and a road map — then return to the Driving Question Board to articulate a complete, evidence-supported answer to the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical hazards. If learners use mobile phones or LDDs to research additional examples, remind them to observe online safety guidelines (KICD PCI: Online Safety) — use school-approved sites only, do not share personal information, and report inappropriate content to the teacher.

LESSONS.overview: Learners work in groups through three real-life application stations — a scale drawing task, a recipe-scaling task (mandazi dough for a school party), and a map-reading task using a Kenyan road map — each of which requires them to choose and apply the correct scale factor (k, k², or k³). Each group then researches one additional real-life example using print or digital resources and delivers a 2-minute presentation to the class. The lesson closes with a full-class return to the Driving Question Board, where learners compose and publicly defend a complete answer to the driving question, explicitly linking evidence from all seven lessons back to the anchoring phenomenon of the uji cups.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners sit in their established groups of 4–5. Each learner silently reads the 'Karibu Catering Challenge' prompt card placed on every desk: 'Mama Wanjiru bakes mandazi for her family using a small round tin of diameter 10 cm. For the Grade 10 end-of-term party she wants to use a similar tin of diameter 20 cm. She plans to mix DOUBLE the amount of dough. Will that be enough? Write your prediction and your reason before we do any calculation.' Learners write individual predictions in their exercise books (3 minutes). The teacher then cold-calls 4 learners — one per group — asking each to state their prediction and the rule they think applies. Predictions are recorded on the board in a T-chart: 'Prediction' | 'Mathematical reason given.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute prompt cards. Say: 'Read silently. Write your own prediction — no group discussion yet. You have 3 minutes.' [Set visible timer.] After 3 minutes: 'Pens down. Let us hear four predictions.' Cold-call Learner 1: 'Tell us your prediction and the one rule from our lessons that supports it.' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call Learner 2, 3, 4 in the same way. Record all predictions verbatim on the board without evaluating them. Say: 'We are going to test every one of these predictions today. Keep them in mind as we work.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Activation of Prior Knowledge (Prediction T-Chart): By committing to a written prediction before calculating, learners surface their current mental model of the k³ rule. Misconceptions — such as 'double the diameter means double the dough' — become visible and productive; the teacher can target them explicitly during the Explain phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each learner has a written prediction with a stated reason in their book before group discussion begins. The teacher scans 4–6 books during cold-calling. Red flag: any learner who predicts 'double the dough is enough' without connecting to a scale-factor rule — note these learners for targeted questioning during Station 2.

framework.learnerExperience:
Groups rotate through three evidence-gathering stations (approximately 8 minutes each, with a 30-second transition signal). Each station has a printed task card and any required materials.

**Station 1 — Scale Drawing (Architecture):** Task card: 'The diagram shows a floor plan of the Mwangaza Primary School staff room. The scale is 1 : 50. (a) Measure the length and width of the room on the diagram in cm. (b) Calculate the actual length and width in metres. (c) A similar staff room at Jua Kali Secondary School is built with all dimensions scaled up by a factor of 1.5. What is the actual floor area of the Jua Kali staff room? How many times larger is it than the Mwangaza room?' Learners record all measurements and calculations on their station worksheet.

**Station 2 — Recipe Scaling (Mandazi for the Party):** Task card: 'Mama Akinyi's small mandazi tin is a cylinder of diameter 10 cm and height 8 cm. The large party tin is similar, with diameter 20 cm. (a) State the linear scale factor k. (b) Mama Akinyi's recipe uses 500 g of flour to fill the small tin. How much flour is needed to fill the large tin? Show which scale factor (k, k², or k³) you used and WHY. (c) If one packet of Blue Band margarine covers the curved surface of the small tin, how many packets cover the curved surface of the large tin?' Learners write working and answers on the worksheet.

**Station 3 — Map Reading (Road Distance):** Task card: 'A printed road-map extract shows the route from Kisumu to Kericho. The map scale is 1 : 500 000. (a) Using a ruler, measure the map distance between the two towns. (b) Calculate the actual road distance in km. (c) A cartographer wants to redraw the map at a scale of 1 : 250 000. By what linear scale factor is the new map enlarged relative to the original? If the area of Lake Victoria on the original map is 12 cm², what will its area be on the new map?' Learners record measurements and calculations on the worksheet.
framework.teacherMoves: Before stations begin, say: 'Each station gives you a real-life problem. Your job is to decide: does this problem need k, k², or k³ — and to show your reasoning, not just the answer. You have 8 minutes per station. I will circulate.' [Start timer.] Circulate continuously. At Station 2, target learners identified in Phase 1 who predicted 'double the dough': ask 'You said double — what is the linear scale factor here? What does that tell you about volume?' [WAIT 12 seconds. Do not answer; redirect to a peer if needed.] At Station 3, prompt: 'What changes when the scale of a map doubles — the distances, the areas, or both? How?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After each 8-minute interval, give a 30-second warning signal ('Finish your current calculation and prepare to move'). After all rotations, say: 'Before we debrief, compare your Station 2 answer to your prediction from Phase 1. Did the mathematics confirm your prediction?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Evidence Stations with Decision-Point Scaffolding: Each station is designed so that learners must explicitly choose between k, k², and k³ rather than following a formula blindly. The three different real-life contexts (architecture, catering, cartography) mirror the unit's central claim — that the same mathematical relationship governs all similar figures — thereby reinforcing the anchoring phenomenon through analogical reasoning across domains.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Station 2 worksheet shows the correct identification of k = 2 and volume scale factor = 8, with 4 000 g (8 × 500 g) of flour; (2) Station 3 worksheet shows correct conversion of map distance to km and correct calculation of new map area as 4 × 12 = 48 cm²; (3) Station 1 worksheet shows correct area scale factor of 1.5² = 2.25. Teacher checks at least one group's worksheet per station during circulation. Red flag: any group using k instead of k³ for the flour quantity in Station 2 — intervene immediately with a pointed question: 'Tell me exactly what the linear scale factor tells us about LENGTH. Now, what does it tell us about VOLUME?'

framework.learnerExperience:
**Part A — Station Debrief (12 minutes):** Each group nominates a spokesperson. The teacher facilitates a whole-class debrief of each station in turn. For Station 2, the teacher explicitly revisits the predictions from Phase 1. Learners who predicted 'double the dough is enough' are asked to explain what they now know. The class agrees on and records the three correct answers in their books.

**Part B — Research & Mini-Presentation Preparation (8 minutes):** Each group uses available print resources (textbooks, newspapers, printed reference sheets) or, where LDDs are available, a vetted digital resource (Kenya Education Cloud or teacher-approved site) to find ONE additional real-life example of similarity and enlargement that they have not yet studied in this unit. Groups prepare a 2-minute spoken presentation: they must name the context, state the linear scale factor, and explain whether the key quantity they are reporting scales by k, k², or k³ — and why. Suggested domains (printed on a 'Research Menu' card): architecture, fashion/tailoring, photography/printing, mapmaking, cooking/baking, packaging design, medical imaging.
framework.teacherMoves:
Station debrief — call on the Station 2 spokesperson first: 'Tell us your answer and which scale factor you used for the flour.' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After the answer, redirect to a learner who predicted 'double': 'Amina, you predicted double. Looking at the mathematics now — what happened?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Validate the moment of surprise: 'This is EXACTLY what happened with the uji cups on Day 1. The cup was twice as tall — but held eight times as much. That was not a mistake. That is k³.' Write on the board: 'k = 2 → Volume scale factor = 2³ = 8 → Need 8 × 500 g = 4 000 g of flour.' For Station 3, cold-call a different group: 'What linear scale factor relates the two maps?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After the correct answer of k = 2, ask: 'So the area of Lake Victoria on the new map will be…?' [WAIT 10 seconds. Cold-call.] Confirm: 'k² = 4, so 4 × 12 = 48 cm².'

For Part B, say: 'You have 8 minutes. Use your Research Menu card. Every person in the group must be able to explain the example — not just the presenter. Choose your presenter now.' Circulate, checking that groups are identifying which scale factor applies to their chosen example. Prompt hesitant groups: 'Is your example about length, surface area, or volume? That tells you which rule to apply.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cognitive Conflict Resolution + Analogical Bridging: The explicit return to the Phase 1 prediction that was wrong ('double the dough') creates productive cognitive conflict. The teacher then bridges this conflict directly to the anchoring phenomenon ('this is exactly what happened with the uji cups'), helping learners consolidate the generalised rule rather than treating each application as a separate case. The Research Menu card extends analogical bridging further across new domains.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) During debrief, at least 3 of 4 groups correctly identify and justify the scale factor for each station; (2) During Part B, each group's Research Menu card has a named example, a stated scale factor, and an identification of k / k² / k³ written before presentations begin. Red flag: a group that cannot articulate why their chosen example uses k² rather than k or k³ — intervene with: 'Describe the quantity you are scaling. Is it a length, an area, or a volume? Now match it to the correct rule.'

framework.learnerExperience:
**Part A — Mini-Presentations (6 minutes):** Each group delivers their 2-minute presentation to the class. The class listens and on a sticky note writes one sentence: 'This example shows [scale factor type] because…' The sticky notes are added to the DQB under a new column headed 'Our Real-Life Evidence — Lesson 7.'

**Part B — DQB Full Revisit (4 minutes):** The teacher draws the class's attention to the entire DQB accumulated across all 7 lessons. Learners look at every column — from 'What we noticed about the uji cups' (Lesson 1) through to 'Our Real-Life Evidence' (today). The teacher poses the driving question in full: 'Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much — and how can we use this mathematical pattern to design, build, and predict the properties of any similar shape or object?' Learners silently draft a complete written answer in their books (3 minutes). One learner is cold-called to read their answer aloud.
framework.teacherMoves: For presentations, use a visible 2-minute timer per group. After each presentation, ask the class: 'Which scale factor did they use — k, k², or k³? Write it on your sticky note and add it to the DQB.' For the DQB full revisit, stand at the board and sweep your hand across all columns: 'Look at how far we have come. Every column answers part of the driving question. Now I want you to write ONE complete answer — use evidence from at least three of our lessons, including today's.' [WAIT 3 minutes writing time. Do not narrate; allow silence.] Cold-call: 'Ochieng, read your answer.' [WAIT 10 seconds before prompting.] After the reading, ask the class: 'What evidence from today's stations would you add to Ochieng's answer?' [Cold-call 2 more learners.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Public Knowledge Construction via DQB Synthesis: The Driving Question Board functions as a visible, cumulative record of the class's collective epistemic journey. By physically viewing all seven lessons' evidence simultaneously and composing a written synthesis, learners perform the metacognitive act of consolidation — moving from fragmented observations (the uji cup surprise) to a generalised, transferable mathematical principle. The mini-presentations add peer-generated evidence to the board, broadening the evidential base beyond teacher-curated examples.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each group's sticky note correctly names a real-life domain, a scale factor type, and a brief reason; (2) In cold-called written answers, learners explicitly name k, k², k³, reference at least one concrete example (e.g., the uji cups or the mandazi tin), and state the general rule. Red flag: a written answer that only restates the rule without evidence — prompt: 'Which of our seven lessons gave you the data that proves this rule? Mention it.'

framework.learnerExperience:
Each learner opens their 'Similarity & Enlargement Model' — the annotated diagram they have been building since Lesson 1 (originally a sketch of the three uji cups with arrows and labels). Today they complete a final revision:
(a) They add a new outer ring or banner to their model titled 'Where This Works in Real Life' and populate it with at least FOUR real-world domains identified across the lesson sequence (e.g., scale drawings, recipe sizing, map reading, packaging, photography).
(b) They write or confirm the three general rules in symbolic and word form inside the model: 'If linear scale factor = k, then area scale factor = k² and volume scale factor = k³.'
(c) They annotate the uji cup diagram — still at the centre of the model — with today's mandazi example: 'e.g., mandazi tin: k = 2 → need k³ = 8 times the dough.'
(d) Learners exchange models with a partner, who checks the three rules are correctly stated and that at least four real-life domains are listed, then signs the model as 'peer-reviewed.'
Learners who finish early write a 'Key Insight' sentence at the bottom of their model: 'The most surprising thing this model shows is…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model has grown with us since Lesson 1 — from a puzzling cup of uji to a full mathematical theory. Today you give it its final layer. Open your models. You have 10 minutes to complete parts (a), (b), and (c).' [Set timer.] Circulate, checking that the three rules are symbolically correct (k, k², k³) and that the real-life domains listed are genuinely diverse. If a learner has only listed cooking examples, prompt: 'What did Station 1 add to your model? What about Station 3?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] After 10 minutes: 'Exchange with a partner. Peer-review for 2 minutes — check the three rules and count the domains. Sign if satisfied.' After peer-review: cold-call one learner to read their 'Key Insight' sentence aloud. Close with: 'From one puzzling cup of uji to a rule that works for every similar shape on earth — that is the power of mathematical modelling. Well done.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Annotated Model Revision (Final Synthesis): The learner's personal, evolving model — anchored throughout by the uji cup diagram — serves as a cognitive artefact that makes the growth of understanding visible and concrete. Adding the 'real-life domains' outer ring in Lesson 7 completes the model's transformation from a description of one phenomenon to a generalisable scientific and mathematical principle. Peer-review introduces a low-stakes accountability structure that reinforces precision in symbolic notation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Completed model contains the three rules in both symbolic and word form (k, k², k³); (2) At least four distinct real-life domains are listed in the outer ring; (3) The uji cup / mandazi annotation is present and numerically correct; (4) Partner's signature is present. Red flag: model still has only the uji cup diagram without any real-life extensions — this learner needs a one-on-one follow-up at the start of Lesson 8 to consolidate generalisation before the summative assessment.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, consider the following questions to guide your preparation for Lesson 8 (the unit summative assessment):
1. During the Phase 1 T-chart, what proportion of learners predicted 'double the dough is enough'? If more than one-third held this misconception entering Lesson 7, build a 5-minute warm-up into Lesson 8 that revisits the k³ rule with a new, rapid example before the assessment begins.
2. In the station debrief, were learners able to articulate WHY they chose k vs. k² vs. k³ — or did they apply the correct rule without being able to justify it? Justification is assessed at the 'Meets Expectations' and above level; if learners can calculate but not explain, provide a sentence-starter scaffold in the assessment: 'I chose this scale factor because…'
3. Which group's mini-presentation showed the most original or surprising real-life example? Consider displaying their example as an extension challenge on the Lesson 8 assessment paper.
4. Review the peer-reviewed models before Lesson 8. Any model missing the symbolic rules (k, k², k³) or with fewer than four real-life domains signals a learner who may need additional support during the assessment. Plan a differentiated prompt card for these learners.
5. Did the DQB synthesis activity produce written answers of sufficient depth? If learners' written answers referenced only one lesson's evidence, plan a brief 'evidence carousel' at the start of Lesson 8 where each group shares their strongest piece of evidence from the unit before the summative task begins.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners measured scale drawings of a school building, calculated flour quantities for a scaled-up mandazi tin (k = 2, requiring 8× the dough), and used a Kisumu–Kericho road map at scale 1:500 000 to calculate real distances and compare map areas at a different scale.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The linear scale factor k governs lengths, k² governs areas (including surface area and map area), and k³ governs volumes (including recipe quantities for similar containers). These three rules apply consistently across all real-life domains — architecture, catering, cartography — involving similar figures or solids.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The uji cup phenomenon — where doubling every dimension of the cup requires 8× as much water to fill it, not 2× — is explained by the k³ volume rule. Because volume depends on three linear dimensions multiplied together, scaling each by k scales the total volume by k × k × k = k³. The same logic explains why Mama Wanjiru needed 4 000 g of flour (not 1 000 g) for the large mandazi tin, and why the Lake Victoria area on a redrawn map at twice the linear scale is 4× larger, not 2×.

LESSONS.title: Project Presentations, Final Explanation & DQB Completion

slo.purpose: Learners synthesise all learning from the unit by presenting their similar-container projects, completing the Driving Question Board, comparing their Day-1 mental model with their final model, and demonstrating mastery of linear, area, and volume scale factors through a written class activity.
slo.knowledge: Properties of similar figures; relationships between linear scale factor k, area scale factor k², and volume scale factor k³; centre of enlargement; application of similarity and enlargement to real-life design.
slo.skills: Measuring and recording dimensions of self-constructed similar containers; calculating and verifying linear, area, and volume scale factors; presenting mathematical reasoning clearly to peers; evaluating peers' work using a rating scale; revising and completing a cumulative explanatory model.
slo.attitudes: Appreciation of the utility and aesthetic value of similarity and enlargement in everyday design; responsibility in taking care of constructed models and instruments; confidence in communicating mathematical ideas; respect for peers' contributions and different approaches.
slo.keyInquiry: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners were puzzled that doubling the height of the uji cup did not double — but quadrupled — the water it held. Over seven lessons they built the mathematical tools to explain this. In Lesson 8 they close the loop: they present containers they made themselves, prove the k / k² / k³ pattern with real measurements, answer every sub-question on the DQB, and write a final individual explanation of the anchoring phenomenon — demonstrating full competency.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners should handle cutting tools (scissors, craft knives) safely when displaying containers. Cardboard edges can be sharp — handle carefully. If glue guns were used in construction, remind learners these are not to be brought into the presentation room.

LESSONS.overview: This is the final lesson of the Similarity and Enlargement unit. It is structured in three connected acts. First (Predict → Observe, ~25 min), learner groups present their self-constructed similar containers — cubes, cuboids, or cylinders made from locally available materials in at least two sizes — and peers evaluate each presentation using a rating scale. Second (Explain → DQB Completion, ~30 min), the whole class conducts a guided final explanation connecting every piece of evidence gathered across Lessons 1–7 back to the anchoring phenomenon (the uji cups), and every sub-question on the Driving Question Board is formally answered and marked. Third (Model Building → Written Assessment, ~25 min), learners individually revise their cumulative model diagram and complete a written class activity that assesses all specific learning outcomes. The lesson culminates with learners articulating — in writing — a complete, mathematically precise answer to the driving question: "Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much?"

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their Lesson-1 written prediction cards (stored in their portfolios) about why the large uji cup needed nine small cups of water to fill it, not three. Working individually for 3 minutes, each learner writes one sentence completing the stem: 'I now know the large uji cup holds nine times as much water because…' They then turn and share with a partner. Selected pairs share with the whole class. Learners also retrieve their Day-1 rough model sketch and place it on their desk alongside the final model page they have been building since Lesson 5.
framework.teacherMoves: Before presentations begin, display the three uji cups (or photographs) at the front — exactly as in Lesson 1. Say: 'We started with a mystery. Before your classmates show us what they built, let's check what you now know.' Distribute the Lesson-1 prediction cards back to learners. Give the 3-minute individual writing time. Then say: 'Turn and tell your partner your sentence.' Allow 90 seconds pair talk. Cold-call 4 learners (aim for gender balance and mixed ability): 'Aisha, please read your sentence.' After each response, WAIT 12 seconds before commenting. Prompt with: 'Can you name the exact scale factor that explains that?' If a learner says 'because the cup is bigger,' push with: 'How much bigger — in area? In volume? What is the mathematical relationship?' Record 3–4 key phrases on the board under the heading 'What we now know'. These will anchor the final explanation later.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Retrieval practice with phenomenon anchoring — by reconnecting to the Lesson-1 uji-cup mystery before presentations, learners activate the full conceptual arc of the unit in working memory, priming them to evaluate peers' projects against the core mathematical ideas (k, k², k³) rather than purely aesthetic criteria.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: each learner's written sentence correctly names at least one of the three scale factor relationships (linear k, area k², volume k³) and connects it to the uji-cup context. Teacher scans sentences during pair-share; learners who write only qualitative statements ('because the cup is bigger') are noted for targeted questioning during the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group (3–4 learners) presents their similar-container project for 4–5 minutes. The presenter must: (1) display the two (or more) containers side by side; (2) read aloud at least two corresponding measurements (e.g., height and diameter for cylinders, or length and width for cuboids); (3) state the linear scale factor k with working shown; (4) calculate the area scale factor k² and the volume scale factor k³ and compare them to actual measured or calculated surface area and volume; (5) describe one challenge faced during construction and how it was resolved. While each group presents, every other learner completes a Peer Rating Scale (four criteria, each scored 1–4): (a) Similar shape clearly demonstrated; (b) Linear scale factor correctly calculated and stated; (c) Area and volume scale factors correctly calculated; (d) Challenge documented and explained. Audience members write one 'warm' comment and one 'wonder' question on a sticky note to hand to the presenting group afterward.
framework.teacherMoves: Seat the class in a horseshoe so all containers are visible. Before the first presentation say: 'Your job as an audience is to be a mathematical critic — not just to admire the container. Use your rating scale. Does their k² match the area ratio? Does k³ match the volume ratio? If not, that is an important finding, not a mistake to hide.' Time each group strictly (use a visible timer). After each presentation, invite one audience question: 'Who has a wonder question for this group?' WAIT 10 seconds. Cold-call if no volunteer. After all groups have presented, ask the whole class: 'Which group's containers showed the k / k² / k³ relationship most clearly — and how do you know?' WAIT 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 different learners. If a group's calculations contain errors, do not correct immediately — note it on the board as 'Let's investigate this together in Phase 3.' For groups presenting cylinders, prompt: 'Your cylinder is just like our uji cups — what does your data say about why the big cylinder holds k³ times as much?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-to-model presentation — learners use their own constructed artefacts as primary evidence, making the abstract relationship k → k² → k³ concrete and verifiable. Peer rating shifts evaluation authority to learners and requires them to apply the mathematical criteria rather than passively receive information. The 'warm/wonder' protocol promotes collaborative, respectful mathematical discourse.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Completed peer rating scales — teacher collects these after presentations to identify which criteria were consistently rated low across groups. (2) Quality of wonder questions — questions that reference specific scale factors (e.g., 'Your k was 2 but your volume ratio was 6 — can you explain?') indicate deeper understanding than aesthetic questions. (3) Teacher notes any group whose stated k² or k³ values are inconsistent with their measurements — these become the focus of targeted correction in Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher leads a whole-class final explanation structured around the uji cups. Learners open their exercise books to a fresh page headed 'Final Explanation'. The teacher works through a summary example on the board using measurements from one of the presented containers (or the uji cups), and learners write their own version simultaneously. The explanation covers: (a) definition and properties of similar figures; (b) determining the centre of enlargement; (c) linear scale factor k from corresponding lengths; (d) area scale factor = k² and why (two dimensions each scaled by k, so area scales by k × k); (e) volume scale factor = k³ and why (three dimensions each scaled by k, so volume scales by k × k × k); (f) a worked example: if a small cylindrical uji cup has radius 4 cm and height 8 cm, and the large cup has radius 8 cm and height 16 cm, find k, the surface area of each cup, and the volume of each cup — then verify that the area ratio equals k² and the volume ratio equals k³. Any calculation errors noted during presentations are resolved collaboratively here: the teacher writes the erroneous result on the board and asks 'What should this be? How do we correct it?' Learners also apply the concept to a new Kenyan context: a small mandazi mould has diameter 5 cm; a large similar mould has diameter 15 cm. What are k, k², and k³? How many small moulds of oil would fill the large mould?
framework.teacherMoves: Begin: 'Let's use what every group showed us to write the most complete explanation we have ever written for this unit.' Work through the uji-cup example step by step on the board, pausing after each step: 'Write this in your own words before I continue.' For the mandazi-mould extension: 'In your book, work out k, k², and k³ for the mandazi moulds. You have 4 minutes.' WAIT for independent work. Cold-call 3 learners to share answers, choosing one who has the correct answer, one who has a partial answer, and one who made an error: 'Kamau, show us your k. Wanjiru, yours was different — walk us through your thinking.' Address any presentation errors from Phase 2 here: 'Group 3 got a volume ratio of 6 when k was 2. Whose volume ratio was different? Let's resolve this together.' Use a targeted question: 'If k = 2, how many times does k appear when we scale volume — think about length, width, height.' WAIT 12 seconds. Do not answer for learners — redirect to a peer if needed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative error analysis with guided note-taking — by deliberately surfacing calculation errors from presentations and resolving them collaboratively, the teacher models mathematical self-correction and deepens procedural understanding. The mandazi-mould extension transfers the concept to a new Kenyan context, testing flexible application beyond the original phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learners' 'Final Explanation' notes — teacher circulates and stamps or ticks books where the uji-cup worked example is correctly completed with all three scale factors verified. (2) Mandazi-mould extension — correct answers: k = 3, k² = 9, k³ = 27; learners who obtain k³ = 27 but cannot explain why demonstrate procedural fluency without conceptual depth — note for written assessment. (3) Learner responses to error-resolution questions — learners who can identify that 'volume uses three dimensions so k appears three times' are demonstrating the target conceptual understanding.

framework.learnerExperience: The class Driving Question Board — maintained since Lesson 1 — is displayed at the front (or projected). It contains the main driving question and all sub-questions learners posted across the unit. The teacher reads each sub-question aloud. For each one, the class decides together: (a) Has this question been fully answered? (b) What is the answer, in one or two precise sentences? A nominated learner writes the agreed answer on a green sticky note and places it over the original question card, completing the DQB. Typical sub-questions that should now be answerable include: 'Why does the area not just double when the lengths double?'; 'What is a scale factor?'; 'Why do architects use scale models?'; 'Is a shadow of a shape similar to the original?'; 'How do manufacturers make containers of different sizes?'; 'What is the centre of enlargement?' If any sub-question remains unanswered, learners note it as an extension question for self-study. Finally, learners re-read the main driving question — 'Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much — and how can we use this mathematical pattern to design, build, and predict the properties of any similar shape or object?' — and vote by show of hands: 'Can we now answer this fully? Yes or No?' The teacher asks two learners who voted Yes to give their answer aloud.
framework.teacherMoves: Stand beside the DQB. 'This board has been our compass since Lesson 1. Every question on it was raised by you. Let's honour that by answering every single one.' Read each sub-question clearly. For each: 'Who can answer this in one precise mathematical sentence? Hands up.' WAIT 10 seconds. If no hand, say: 'Think back to the lesson where we first found evidence for this.' After a learner responds, ask: 'Does everyone agree? Thumbs up / thumbs sideways / thumbs down.' For disagreements, facilitate briefly: 'Two different answers — which one uses the correct mathematical language?' For the final driving question vote, cold-call one Yes voter and one learner who hesitated: 'Tell me the part you are still unsure about.' Use this to bridge to the written assessment: 'The written activity will give you a chance to show me in detail exactly where you are with all of this.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board synthesis — a public, collaborative closure of the inquiry arc. By requiring precise one-sentence answers (not vague summaries), the protocol forces learners to consolidate knowledge into transferable propositions. The vote on the driving question surfaces residual uncertainty and frames the written assessment as meaningful rather than arbitrary.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Quality of green-sticky-note answers — well-formed answers name the scale factor algebraically (e.g., 'Area scales by k² because two linear dimensions are each multiplied by k'). Vague answers ('because it gets bigger') signal incomplete understanding and are sent back for revision before being posted. (2) Thumbs vote during discussion — widespread thumbs-sideways on a specific sub-question alerts the teacher to a concept that may need brief re-teaching before or during the written activity. (3) DQB is now fully green — all sub-questions answered; any remaining orange cards are recorded by the teacher for follow-up.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners first spend 5 minutes revising their cumulative model diagram (built progressively since Lesson 5). They add a final layer: a labelled arrow from 'linear scale factor k' branching into 'area scale factor k²' and 'volume scale factor k³', each with a real-number example from their own project. They also annotate one feature of their diagram that was wrong or incomplete in Lesson 1 and write beside it: 'I used to think… Now I know…'. They then complete a written class activity (individual, 15 minutes) comprising the following tasks: (1) Two similar cuboid water tanks used on Rift Valley farms — Tank A: 50 cm × 40 cm × 30 cm; Tank B has all dimensions scaled by k = 2.5. Find (a) the dimensions of Tank B, (b) the surface area of each tank and the area scale factor, (c) the volume of each tank and the volume scale factor, (d) the number of 20-litre jerricans needed to fill Tank B if Tank A holds exactly 2 jerricans. (2) A label designer in Nairobi wraps a cylindrical tin of radius 6 cm and height 10 cm. A similar larger tin has radius 9 cm. Find the linear scale factor, the area of the label for each tin (curved surface area only), and verify the area ratio equals k². (3) Short answer: In your own words, explain why doubling all dimensions of a container multiplies its volume by 8, not 2. Use the uji-cup story in your answer.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the written activity sheet. Say: 'This is individual work. Your model diagram is also individual. You may look at your notes and Final Explanation page.' Circulate throughout. After 8 minutes, give a quiet prompt: 'If you are on question 1(d), check: how many jerricans does Tank B hold? Remember k³.' Do not give answers — redirect with questions. With 3 minutes remaining, say: 'Finish question 3 even if question 2 is incomplete — your explanation in words is as important as your calculations.' Collect activity sheets. Before dismissal, ask the class to hold up their model diagrams: 'Look at your Lesson-1 sketch and your final model side by side. What is the single biggest change in your thinking?' Cold-call 3 learners for a one-sentence response. Close with: 'The uji cups were not a mystery — they were mathematics. You now own that mathematics.' Remind learners to store their constructed containers safely as they may be used as teaching resources.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model revision with 'I used to think / Now I know' metacognitive annotation — this explicitly surfaces conceptual change, helping learners consolidate the difference between their naive understanding (scaling is linear) and their final scientific model (scaling is dimensional: k, k², k³). The written assessment is deliberately multi-representational: numerical calculation, formula application, and explanatory prose — mirroring the KICD assessment rubric levels.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Model diagrams — a complete final model shows k → k² → k³ with a real-number example and a correctly annotated 'I used to think / Now I know' statement. (2) Written activity — mark scheme: Q1(a) 125 cm × 100 cm × 75 cm; Q1(b) SA of A = 9,400 cm², SA of B = 58,750 cm², ratio = 6.25 = k²; Q1(c) Vol A = 60,000 cm³, Vol B = 937,500 cm³, ratio = 15.625 = k³; Q1(d) Tank A holds 2 jerricans so Tank B holds 2 × 15.625 = 31.25 ≈ 32 jerricans (rounding up); Q2 k = 1.5, label A = 120π cm², label B = 270π cm², ratio = 270π/120π = 2.25 = k²; Q3 — assessed on: names k = 2, states each of 3 dimensions doubles so volume multiplies 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, connects explicitly to the uji cup. (3) Exceeds-expectation indicator: learner in Q1(d) explains that partial jerricans are not practical and rounds up, demonstrating real-life application judgment.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions before planning any remediation or extension:
1. PROJECT QUALITY — Did all groups correctly state and verify all three scale factors (k, k², k³) using their own measurements? If more than two groups had incorrect volume scale factor calculations, plan a 10-minute consolidation activity in the next available lesson using fresh examples from Kenyan packaging (e.g., Bidco cooking oil tins in 500 ml, 1 L, and 2 L sizes).
2. DQB GAPS — Were there any sub-questions on the DQB that the class could not answer confidently? Note these and include them as starter questions in the next strand's first lesson to reinforce cross-topic connections.
3. WRITTEN ASSESSMENT — Review the collected activity sheets before the next lesson. Tally the number of learners who: (a) correctly completed all three scale factor calculations; (b) correctly completed Q1 and Q2 but could not write the Q3 explanation in their own words; (c) completed fewer than two questions successfully. Group (b) may need guided writing support; Group (c) may require a structured re-teach of the k / k² / k³ relationships before the sub-strand is formally closed.
4. MODEL PROGRESSION — Compare the Lesson-1 sketches and final models. Were the 'I used to think / Now I know' annotations specific and mathematical, or vague? Specific annotations (e.g., 'I used to think doubling size doubled volume; now I know volume scales by k³ = 8') indicate deep conceptual change. Vague annotations signal that the learner has procedural fluency but has not fully restructured their prior understanding — follow up with a one-on-one conversation.
5. EQUITY OBSERVATION — During presentations, note which learners were consistently silent or rated by peers as below expectations. Were there learners whose constructed containers showed strong practical skill but weak written calculation? These learners may benefit from oral assessment as a supplementary approach.
6. PHENOMENON CLOSURE — Did every learner articulate — at least once, orally or in writing — a complete answer to the driving question that named k, k², and k³? The uji-cup mystery should feel fully resolved. If learners still express surprise or uncertainty about the nine-small-cups result, this is a signal that the volume scale factor conceptual link was not sufficiently consolidated across the unit.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed their own peer-constructed similar containers (cubes, cuboids, cylinders) made from locally available materials in at least two sizes. They measured corresponding dimensions side by side, saw with their own hands that every length scaled by the same factor k, and verified (or discovered errors in) their calculated surface area ratios and volume ratios. They also re-observed the three uji cups from Lesson 1 — now able to explain precisely why nine small cups of water, not three, are needed to fill the large cup.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners consolidated that: (1) similar figures have equal corresponding angles and proportional corresponding sides; (2) the linear scale factor k is the ratio of any pair of corresponding lengths; (3) the area scale factor is always k² — because area involves two linear dimensions each scaled by k; (4) the volume scale factor is always k³ — because volume involves three linear dimensions each scaled by k; (5) these relationships apply universally to all similar figures and solids, including the containers they designed and built themselves; (6) real-life applications include container manufacturing, architectural scale models, map-making, and packaging design.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained — through project presentations, peer rating, collaborative DQB closure, final model annotation, and individual written tasks — why doubling all linear dimensions of any container multiplies its surface area by 4 (= 2²) and its volume by 8 (= 2³). They connected this explanation back to the anchoring phenomenon: the large uji cup has k = 3 relative to the small cup, so its cross-sectional area is k² = 9 times larger (explaining why nine small cups fill it) and its volume is k³ = 27 times larger. They demonstrated this understanding using their own constructed containers and novel Kenyan contexts (Rift Valley water tanks, Nairobi label design, mandazi moulds), satisfying the KICD key inquiry question: How is similarity and enlargement applied in real life?

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Essential Mathematics – Grade 10 | Sub-strand 2.1: Similarity and Enlargement
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions:
This is your Final Explanation task. You have spent 8 lessons investigating the "Shrinking Uji Cup" phenomenon — discovering why doubling every dimension of a container makes it hold eight times as much, not two times. Now it is your turn to bring all of your learning together into one well-reasoned, evidence-based explanation.

READ THE DRIVING QUESTION CAREFULLY:
"Why does doubling the size of a container make it hold eight times as much — and how can we use this mathematical pattern to design, build, and predict the properties of any similar shape or object?"

YOUR TASK:
Answer the driving question fully by completing each section below. In every section, connect your mathematical reasoning back to the uji cups from the class demonstration, AND apply your understanding to a new real-life Kenyan context. Use diagrams, calculations, or tables wherever they strengthen your explanation.

TIPS FOR SUCCESS:
• Show all working — a correct answer without reasoning earns fewer marks.
• Use precise mathematical vocabulary: scale factor, linear scale factor (k), area scale factor (k²), volume scale factor (k³), similar figures, enlargement, ratio, proportion.
• Make your explanation clear enough that a fellow Grade 10 student who missed the lessons could read it and understand the big idea.
• Check your calculations at least once before submitting.

sections.title: Section 1: The Mystery of the Uji Cups — Identifying the Pattern
sections.prompt: Describe what was observed with the three uji cups. Explain what a linear scale factor (k) is, and use measurements or a table to show how the height and diameter of the cups are related. Then state — in your own words — why filling the larger cup required more water than most people expected. What is the mathematical pattern at the heart of this mystery?
sections.exemplar:
When our class measured the three uji cups — the toddler cup, the adult mug, and the catering flask — we found that every dimension of the adult mug was exactly twice the corresponding dimension of the toddler cup, and every dimension of the catering flask was exactly three times the toddler cup's dimensions. This multiplying value is called the linear scale factor, k. For the mug, k = 2; for the flask, k = 3.

A table of measurements might look like this:
| Cup | Height (cm) | Diameter (cm) | k (compared to toddler cup) |
|-------------|-------------|---------------|------------------------------|
| Toddler | 6 | 4 | 1 |
| Adult mug | 12 | 8 | 2 |
| Catering flask | 18 | 12 | 3 |

Most people expected the adult mug to hold twice as much water as the toddler cup, because 'twice as big' sounds like 'twice as much.' But this thinking only applies to one dimension (length). A cylinder has THREE dimensions that all scale at the same time. The cross-sectional area (a circle) scales by k² = 4, and the volume scales by k³ = 8. So the adult mug holds 4 times as much water as the toddler cup, and the catering flask holds 27 times as much — not 3 times. The mathematical pattern is: when you scale every linear dimension by k, areas scale by k² and volumes scale by k³.

sections.title: Section 2: The Mathematics of Scaling — Proving Why k, k², and k³ Work
sections.prompt: Using the formulae for a cylinder (or any shape of your choice), prove algebraically why scaling every length by a factor of k causes area to scale by k² and volume to scale by k³. Show full working. Then verify your proof using the actual numbers from the uji cup demonstration (k = 2 and k = 3).
sections.exemplar:
Let the toddler cup have radius r and height h.

Its cross-sectional area is: A₁ = πr²
Its curved surface area is: CSA₁ = 2πrh
Its volume is: V₁ = πr²h

Now scale every linear dimension by k. The new cup has radius kr and height kh.

New cross-sectional area: A₂ = π(kr)² = πk²r² = k² × A₁ ✓
New curved surface area: CSA₂ = 2π(kr)(kh) = 2πk²rh = k² × CSA₁ ✓
New volume: V₂ = π(kr)²(kh) = πk²r² × kh = πk³r²h = k³ × V₁ ✓

This algebraic proof works for ANY shape, not just cylinders, because every area formula contains exactly two linear dimensions multiplied together (giving k²), and every volume formula contains exactly three linear dimensions multiplied together (giving k³).

Verification with the uji cups:
• For k = 2 (toddler → adult mug): Area scales by 2² = 4 ✓ (we needed 4 cups of water to fill the cross-section), Volume scales by 2³ = 8 ✓
• For k = 3 (toddler → catering flask): Area scales by 3² = 9 ✓ (the label requires 9 times as much paper), Volume scales by 3³ = 27 ✓

The algebra and the physical experiment agree perfectly, which gives us strong confidence in the rule.

sections.title: Section 3: Applying the Pattern — Similarity in a Kenyan Context
sections.prompt: Choose ONE real-life Kenyan context (for example: a farmer in Kericho designing water storage tanks of different sizes; a jua kali artisan in Kamukunji making sufurias of similar shapes; a baker in Mombasa scaling up a mandazi recipe using similar baking tins; or an architect in Nairobi scaling a building model). Describe the context, identify the linear scale factor, and then calculate at least TWO of the following: the new surface area, the new volume, or the new capacity. Show all working and explain what your answer means in practical terms.
sections.exemplar:
Context: A jua kali artisan in Kamukunji, Nairobi makes aluminium sufurias (cooking pots) in similar cylindrical shapes. The small sufuria has a radius of 10 cm and a height of 12 cm. The large family sufuria is similar to the small one, with a linear scale factor of k = 2.5.

Step 1 – Find the dimensions of the large sufuria:
Radius: 10 × 2.5 = 25 cm
Height: 12 × 2.5 = 30 cm

Step 2 – Calculate the surface area scale factor:
Area scale factor = k² = 2.5² = 6.25
Small sufuria total surface area = 2πr(r + h) = 2π(10)(10 + 12) = 2π(10)(22) = 440π ≈ 1,382 cm²
Large sufuria total surface area = 6.25 × 440π = 2,750π ≈ 8,639 cm²
Practical meaning: The artisan needs 6.25 times as much aluminium sheet to make the large sufuria. This helps him price the larger pot correctly — it costs far more than 2.5 times the small one.

Step 3 – Calculate the volume scale factor:
Volume scale factor = k³ = 2.5³ = 15.625
Small sufuria volume = πr²h = π(10)²(12) = 1,200π ≈ 3,770 cm³ ≈ 3.77 litres
Large sufuria volume = 15.625 × 1,200π = 18,750π ≈ 58,905 cm³ ≈ 58.9 litres
Practical meaning: The large sufuria holds about 15.6 times as much food as the small one — enough to cook githeri for a large community gathering, not just a small family.

sections.title: Section 4: Working Backwards — Finding the Scale Factor from Area or Volume
sections.prompt: Sometimes you know the area ratio or volume ratio, but you need to find the linear scale factor. Explain how to work backwards from k² or k³ to find k. Then solve this problem fully: A water tank manufacturer in Kisumu produces two similar tanks. The smaller tank has a capacity of 500 litres. The larger tank has a capacity of 4,000 litres. (a) Find the volume scale factor. (b) Find the linear scale factor, k. (c) If the smaller tank has a total surface area of 3.2 m², find the surface area of the larger tank.
sections.exemplar:
To work backwards from a volume ratio to find k, you take the cube root: k = ∛(volume scale factor). To work backwards from an area ratio to find k, you take the square root: k = √(area scale factor). This is the reverse of what we proved in Section 2.

Solution:
(a) Volume scale factor = larger volume ÷ smaller volume = 4,000 ÷ 500 = 8

(b) Linear scale factor: k³ = 8, so k = ∛8 = 2
The larger tank has every linear dimension exactly twice that of the smaller tank.

(c) Area scale factor = k² = 2² = 4
Surface area of larger tank = 4 × 3.2 m² = 12.8 m²

Interpretation: The manufacturer in Kisumu needs 4 times as much material (metal sheeting or plastic) to build the large tank as the small one, even though the large tank holds 8 times as much water. This is an important business insight — material costs scale by k², but storage capacity scales by k³, so larger tanks are more cost-efficient per litre of water stored. This is why big water storage projects (like those supplying Kisumu or Nairobi estates) use the largest tanks possible.

sections.title: Section 5: Connecting Back to the Driving Question — Your Final Model
sections.prompt: Answer the driving question directly and completely, using everything you have learned across all 8 lessons. Your answer must: (1) Explain WHY doubling every dimension leads to 8 times the volume (not 2 times). (2) State the general rule for any scale factor k. (3) Explain how this pattern can be used to DESIGN, BUILD, and PREDICT properties of similar shapes. (4) Reflect on one thing this unit changed about how you see the world around you in Kenya.
sections.exemplar:
Doubling the size of a container makes it hold eight times as much — not two times — because volume depends on THREE dimensions (length × width × height, or radius² × height). When you double every single dimension, each of the three dimensions is multiplied by 2, so the total volume is multiplied by 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8. You cannot just double the volume by doubling one measurement; all dimensions scale together.

The General Rule:
For any two similar shapes or solids with linear scale factor k:
• Corresponding lengths scale by k (e.g., all sides, heights, radii, perimeters)
• Corresponding areas scale by k² (e.g., cross-sections, surface areas, footprints)
• Corresponding volumes (and capacities) scale by k³

Using the Pattern to Design, Build, and Predict:
Design: An architect in Nairobi designing a scale model of a building at 1:50 scale knows that every real dimension is 50 times the model dimension. The real building's floor area is 50² = 2,500 times the model's floor area, and its volume is 50³ = 125,000 times the model's volume. She can predict these values without ever leaving her office.
Build: A jua kali artisan making similar-shaped pots of different sizes can calculate exactly how much aluminium sheet is needed for each size (using k²) and how much each pot will hold (using k³), reducing waste and improving pricing.
Predict: Engineers designing water tanks, fuel storage containers, or grain silos across Kenya can use k³ to predict capacity and k² to estimate material costs — making projects cheaper and more efficient.

Personal Reflection:
Before this unit, I assumed that if something looked 'twice as big,' it held twice as much. Now I realise that our everyday language about size is misleading — 'twice as big' usually means twice as tall or twice as wide, but the volume grows much faster than that. When I walk through a market in Nairobi and see large and small versions of the same container, I now automatically think: what is k? And then k² and k³ follow immediately. This unit has genuinely changed the way I see and question the physical world.
